# 1 Goals & Executive Summary: Applied Analytics for Maintenance Operations

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(here)
library(tidyr)
```

```{r}
#| label: ingest
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

boston_311 <- read_csv(here("data", "tmpm461rr5o.csv"))
```

## 1.1 Goals

This report illustrates the value of applying Data Science (DS) and Operations Research (OR) methodologies to extract operational intelligence from service request databases. Managing large-scale property portfolios—spanning hundreds of buildings and thousands of service requests—requires more than descriptive dashboards. Reporting metrics like average completion times or SLA (Service Level Agreement) compliance rates frequently mask underlying bottlenecks. Instead, deeper analysis of this data can shed light on these bottlenecks and identify targeted opportunities to improve service delivery.

## 1.2 The Example Dataset (Boston 311)

To demonstrate the application of these methodologies, this report utilizes the publicly available Boston 311 (Year 2024) dataset as an applied proxy. Boston’s geographic districts and digital queues serve as a practical analog for decentralized property management. Just as a real estate portfolio is divided into building subsets managed by local teams, the city's workload is distributed across distinct neighborhoods. By treating constituent requests as tenant service orders, this dataset provides a relevant case study.

## 1.3 Key findings

By applying Data Science and Operations Research methods to the 2024 dataset (242,033 closed records and 40,802 open records), we isolated operational drivers of municipal service. Because standard reporting metrics can be misleading in maintenance environments, this analysis relies on robust, non-parametric statistics and machine learning to address these limitations and uncover the following insights:

**Major Disruptions & Cumulative Backlogs**: Visualizing unresolved tickets revealed backlog peaks at 60 and 170 days (@fig-open-tickets-distribution). Because visual peaks can be artifacts of data binning, we confirmed their existence using the non-parametric *Hartigan’s Dip Test*, yielding an effect size and p-value that ruled out random chance (@fig-robust-binning). Cross-referencing these spikes by `department` showed they were not general trends, but instead localized to bottlenecks in the Transportation Department's (`BTD`) queue (@fig-open-tickets-by-month). These surges align with major infrastructure events in 2024: the Sumner Tunnel Restoration Project (June) and the Orange Line shutdown (October).

**The Right-Skew Flaw & Organizational Routing**: Service completion times are right-skewed and do not fit a normal distribution, even after logarithmic transformation (@fig-resolution-density-log). Consequently, relying on average (mean) completion times distorts performance metrics. Using a volume-weighted K-S test to analyze *Service Level Agreement (SLA)* closures (@fig-sla-delta-distribution), results indicate that resolution compliance is more associated with functional organizational routing—such as the digital `queue` and task type—than with geographic factors like `zipcode`, `ward`, or `neighborhood` (@tbl-factor-ranking, @fig-factor-ranking-lollipop). These digital routing assignments are not just administrative tags; they define the physical task and the assigned personnel. Because task type reflects the complexity of the work, organizational routing functions as the primary structural driver of SLA compliance.

**AI-Driven Text Analytics**: The dataset contains a large volume of unstructured free text (`closure_reason`). Initially, we deployed an unsupervised AI clustering pipeline to extract operational bottlenecks (@fig-plot-bertopic-results), which a locally hosted LLM then translated into broader thematic categories (@tbl-llm-topic-translation, @fig-plot-bertopic-results-after-ollama). Statistical testing confirmed these AI-generated topics are concentrated within specific departments (@fig-topic-factor-enrichment). However, because unsupervised AI struggles to separate operational signals from administrative noise (e.g., "arrived," "completed"), it did not accurately map granular organizational and seasonal shifts.

To address this, we developed a deterministic text compression pipeline (Section 2.5.2). We utilized *Expected Mutual Information (EMI)* as a mathematical filter to remove repetitive administrative words and isolate the dataset's core structural vocabulary (@fig-emi-distribution). We then applied *Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI)* to extract the vocabulary specific to individual departments (@tbl-pmi-departments) and seasons for the Public Works department (@tbl-pwdx-seasonal-all). Direct human inspection of these filtered word arrays can provide immediate and clear operational insight without the need for further AI processing.

While feeding these isolated arrays to a local LLM can generate concise physical operational profiles (@tbl-llm-profiles), this final generative step requires strict oversight. The LLM produces stable, accurate translations *only when constrained by concrete, task-oriented nouns with large PMI values*. If the extracted vocabulary contains abstract or behavioral terms, the model exhibits generative volatility, potentially synthesizing conflicting narratives across identical prompts (@tbl-llm-seasonal-profiles-1, @tbl-llm-seasonal-profiles-2). This hybrid methodology—anchoring Generative AI with statistical filtering and human expertise—promises transferable and interesting applications for property management databases (Section 1.4).

**Workforce Velocity (Survival Analysis)**: Standard average completion times suffer from survivorship bias because they only account for resolved tickets, ignoring the aging backlog of open requests. To provide a more accurate measure of true workforce velocity, we applied Kaplan-Meier survival curves (@fig-survival-analysis-departments) to model how departments process their entire queues over time:

- *Public Works (`PWDx`)*: Demonstrates a rapid triage model, clearing 80–85% of tickets within 48 to 72 hours.

- *Baseline (`BTDT`, `INFO`, `ISD`)*: Clears approximately 75% of tickets within a week, followed by a steady resolution rate for the remainder.

- *Parks & Recreation (`PARK`)*: Exhibits a structural bottleneck. The survival curve flatlines, with roughly 20% of tickets remaining unresolved past the 60-day mark.

To complement the Kaplan-Meier estimates and isolate specific factors influencing resolution speed, we utilized Cox Proportional Hazards modeling. The adjusted model (@fig-cox-regression-model-adjusted) indicates that `PWDx` operates at nearly double the baseline speed, whereas `PARK` operates at a 35% deficit. Additionally, manual ticket intake (constituent phone calls, `INFO`) introduces administrative friction, slowing the resolution pipeline by approximately 22% compared to digital submissions.

**Queueing Dynamics & Budget Cycles**: Unlike survival analysis, which tracks the aging of individual tickets, queueing analysis measures overall system responsiveness by tracking input versus resolution rates (@fig-queue-velocity-analysis). The data shows that `PWDx` and `INFO` operate reactive systems, managing sudden volume spikes and recovering quickly. Conversely, `PARK` exhibits queue instability during the first six months of the year, accumulating a consistent backlog due to a deficit in daily capacity. A significant queue reduction in July aligns with the start of the municipal Fiscal Year, suggesting a reliance on seasonal budget allocations or temporary workforce expansion. Additionally, a single-day 1,500-ticket closure event in the Transportation Department (`BTD`) indicates an administrative batch-processing artifact rather than physical task completion.

**Spatial Autocorrelation & Logistical Friction**: While flat geographical categories (such as zip codes or wards) show relatively small effect sizes compared to organizational routing, relying solely on categorical bins can obscure underlying physical topology. By applying continuous spatial autocorrelation (@fig-spatial-equity-morans-i), the *Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA)* analysis maps localized variations in service times (@fig-spatial-equity-lisa). The model identifies three "High-High" clusters (areas with elevated completion times) located further from the city's central core: *Allston-Brighton*, *East Boston*, and *Charlestown*. This pattern indicates that physical distance and infrastructure chokepoints introduce logistical friction for field teams dispatching to these neighborhoods. Conversely, faster resolution times ("Low-Low" clusters) are concentrated in the downtown core, likely reflecting the operational efficiency of proximity to centralized staging areas.

## 1.4 Potential Transferability to Property Management

While this report leverages a municipal dataset, the mathematical framework is partly transferable to large-scale property maintenance. Decentralized real estate portfolios face similar structural challenges regarding resource allocation, physical dependencies, and workforce capacity. For example:

- **Queueing Theory & Labor Scaling**: Comparing the queue velocity of different geographic property subsets allows directors to identify if specific on-site maintenance teams are structurally overwhelmed, ensuring labor is scaled to match actual inbound tenant demand rather than arbitrary building counts.

- **Survival Analysis & Regulatory Readiness**: Probabilistic modeling via Kaplan-Meier and Cox Hazards can track the resolution of complex capital repairs versus routine maintenance, ensuring critical safety issues are resolved well before they trigger regulatory scoring deductions (such as inspection breaches).

- **Spatial Autocorrelation for Logistical Friction**: Just as municipal infrastructure creates chokepoints, travel time between scattered-site properties introduces massive logistical friction. Spatial analysis mathematically isolates which buildings suffer from delayed service maybe due to their geographic locations.

- **Text Analytics & Generative AI**: Unsupervised clustering of tenant work orders can provide broad thematic overviews, but applying the deterministic text compression pipeline (EMI/PMI) functions as a universal contrast engine capable of extracting highly targeted, granular intelligence. By altering the mathematical partition within a maintenance database, this framework unlocks the following potential applications:

  - **Technician & Crew Profiling**: Partitioning text data by maintenance staff mathematically isolates the distinct operational footprint of specific technicians, and might highlight specialized skill sets, pinpoint training gaps, or reveal differing behavioral approaches to resolving identical maintenance issues.
  
  - **Regulatory Risk & Inspection Modeling**: Partitioning properties by historical regulatory outcomes isolates the exact semantic vocabulary that precedes failed regulatory standards (e.g., NSPIRE). This might map structural maintenance dependencies, acting as a direct empirical input for models that attempt to predict inspection scores.

- **Workflow Dependencies & Administrative Friction**: Analyzing service metadata can reveal non-trivial operational dependencies that standard reporting misses. For example, this report demonstrated how the initial method of ticket intake (manual constituent phone calls handled by `INFO` versus direct digital submissions) introduces administrative friction that slows down downstream physical resolution times by roughly 22%, highlighting how digital bottlenecks impact field workflows.

- **Administrative Cycles & Capacity Dependencies**: Analytics can uncover how physical field workflows are dependent on non-physical administrative cycles. For example, queueing analysis in this report revealed that the `PARK` department lacks baseline daily capacity and instead rely on the July 1st start of the municipal Fiscal Year [(Boston.gov)](https://www.boston.gov/departments/city-council/fy2027-city-council-legislative-budget-review) to fund the workforce unlocks necessary to clear their accumulated backlogs.

Ultimately, applying Data Science—specifically the descriptive and diagnostic analytics branches of Operations Research—to service request databases extracts operational intelligence, moving beyond basic dashboards to reveal true workforce capacity and structural bottlenecks.

## 1.5 The Need for a Human Expert

Extracting this level of intelligence is not a matter of automated, plug-and-play software. It requires iterative analytical detective work that relies on three core methodological pillars:

**Statistical Rigor**: Averages are mathematically flawed in maintenance data due to survivorship bias and right-skewed extremes that prohibit normal assumptions. Robust probabilistic modeling is required to measure performance and system stability, necessitating statistical expertise.

**Data Forensics**: Every operational dataset contains administrative artifacts, batch-processing illusions, and mislabeled text. Identifying these anomalies and selecting the appropriate statistical models requires an exploratory process that generalized software cannot fully automate.

**Advanced Programming**: Moving beyond spreadsheets to deploy multivariate regressions, spatial autocorrelation, and localized machine learning pipelines is essential. While AI-aided programming accelerates this process, it still requires architectural understanding and practical implementation experience.

This statistically rigorous and advanced forensic work is detailed in the next section.

# 2 Analytical Forensics: Detailed Findings and Methodology.

## 2.1 Data Validation and Cohort Partitioning

We first implement an audit script to map column types, quantify unique values, and identify missing records (NAs). This step prevents errors in downstream modeling and generates the interactive data dictionary below.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-data-dictionary
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Dataset Overview: Column types, unique values, and missing data."

library(dplyr)
library(DT)

# 1. Overall dimensions
cat("Dataset Dimensions:", format(nrow(boston_311), big.mark = ","), "rows and", ncol(boston_311), "columns.\n\n")
# 2. Column-summary dataframe
data_summary <- tibble(
  Column = names(boston_311),
  Type = sapply(boston_311, function(x) paste(class(x), collapse = ", ")),
  Unique_Values = sapply(boston_311, n_distinct),
  Missing_Values = sapply(boston_311, function(x) sum(is.na(x)))
)
# 3. Interactive HTML table
datatable(
  data_summary,
  rownames = FALSE,
  options = list(
    pageLength = 10, 
    autoWidth = TRUE,
    dom = 'tp' # Keeps the interface clean (just table and pagination)
  ),
  caption = "Dataset Overview: Column types, unique values, and missing data."
)
```

Following the audit, we partition the raw data into two distinct operational cohorts. This separation is necessary because open and closed tickets represent fundamentally different system states:

**Backlog Cohort (Open Requests)**: Work orders unresolved at the end of the observation period. This subset provides a diagnostic snapshot to evaluate system capacity and bottlenecks at a fixed point in time.

**Resolved Cohort (Closed Requests)**: Work orders with a complete lifecycle. This dataset is used to evaluate workforce speed, logistical friction, and SLA compliance.

To address administrative noise in the raw data, we apply a filtering pipeline to the Resolved Cohort. The validation script calculates the resolution time (in days) for every closed ticket, isolates temporal features (month, weekday, and hour of intake) for seasonality analysis, and removes invalid entries—such as negative resolution times caused by clerical data-entry errors.

```{r}
#| label: data-cleaning
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

# Ingestion
boston_311 <- read_csv(here("data", "tmpm461rr5o.csv"))

# Step 1: Base Filtering and Feature Engineering
boston_mutated <- boston_311 %>%
  # Filter for completed work orders
  filter(case_status == "Closed", !is.na(closed_dt), !is.na(open_dt)) %>%
  mutate(
    # Exact resolution time
    resolution_days = as.numeric(difftime(closed_dt, open_dt, units = "days")),
    # Temporal features for seasonality and scheduling analysis
    open_month = month(open_dt, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE),
    open_wday = wday(open_dt, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE, week_start = 1), # Monday = 1
    open_hour = hour(open_dt)
  )

# Step 2: Quantify the data entry errors
negative_records_count <- sum(boston_mutated$resolution_days < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

# Step 3: Purge errors and finalize the Resolved Cohort
boston_clean <- boston_mutated %>%
  filter(resolution_days >= 0)

write_csv(boston_clean, here("data", "boston_clean.csv"))

# Output the validation summary
cat("Purged", format(negative_records_count, big.mark = ","), "records with negative resolution times (data entry errors).\n")
cat("Cleaned dataset contains", format(nrow(boston_clean), big.mark = ","), "closed records ready for analysis.\n")
```

Before examining the Resolved Cohort, we analyze the Backlog Cohort to assess the municipal queue at the close of 2024.

## 2.2 Backlog Diagnostics: Detecting Major Disruptions

Having partitioned the data, we first examine the Backlog Cohort. Analyzing unresolved requests demonstrates how to statistically validate visual patterns and identify major operational disruptions.

By querying the dataset for work orders active on December 31, 2024, the pipeline identifies over 40,000 open records and calculates the calendar age of each pending ticket.

```{r}
#| label: isolate-open-cases
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

# Tickets still open at the end of 2024
boston_open <- boston_311 %>%
  filter(case_status == "Open" | is.na(closed_dt)) %>%
  mutate(
    open_month = month(open_dt, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE),
    # Ticket age as of the end of the 2024 calendar year
    days_open_at_yearend = as.numeric(difftime(as.POSIXct("2024-12-31 23:59:59"), open_dt, units = "days"))
  )
write_csv(boston_open, here("data", "boston_open.csv"))
# Short output
cat("Isolated", format(nrow(boston_open), big.mark = ","), "open records.\n\n")
```

@fig-open-tickets-distribution below overlays a density curve on top of a weekly-binned histogram. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-open-tickets-distribution
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Age distribution of open requests at the end of 2024."

ggplot(boston_open, aes(x = days_open_at_yearend)) +
  # Histogram with a 7-day binwidth to represent weekly operational cycles
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 7, fill = "lightgray", color = "white") +
  # Density overlay to highlight the overall shape and search for bimodality
  geom_density(color = "darkred", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 365, by = 60)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution of Open Requests at Year-End",
    subtitle = "Investigating bimodality: Active recent backlog vs. stagnant long-term requests.",
    x = "Days Open (as of Dec 31, 2024)",
    y = "Density (Proportion of Open Work Orders)"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

Visual inspection suggests distinct peaks in the backlog age, specifically around 60 and 170 days. A standard analytical step is determining whether these represent structural trends (such as a seasonal surge) or statistical artifacts caused by "binning bias"—the chosen width of the histogram buckets.

Because our sample size is large, we can evaluate the stability of this observation by altering the histogram resolution. If the peaks are structural, they will persist whether the data is grouped by day, week, or month.

@fig-robust-binning demonstrates that the peaks at 60 and 170 days are stable and not binning artifacts. However, because this observation still relies on visual inspection, we must apply a formal statistical test to mathematically confirm their presence.

```{r}
#| label: fig-robust-binning
#| fig-subcap: true
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Histograms of age distribution of open requests at the end of 2024, with different bin sizes: (a) days, (b) weeks and (c) months."

# Base plot for the first two charts mapping continuous days
p_base <- ggplot(boston_open, aes(x = days_open_at_yearend)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 365, by = 120)) +
  labs(x = "Days Open (as of Dec 31)", y = "Volume of Open Tickets") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"))
# Daily Binning
p_base + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "darkgray", color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  labs(title = "Daily Resolution (1-Day Bins)")
# Weekly Binning
p_base + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 7, fill = "steelblue", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  labs(title = "Weekly Resolution (7-Day Bins)")
# Calendar Months
boston_open %>%
  # Reverse the month levels so December (newest) is on the left, matching the 0-365 days flow
  mutate(open_month_rev = factor(open_month, levels = rev(levels(open_month)))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = open_month_rev)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "darkred", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly Resolution (Calendar)",
    x = "Month Opened (Newest to Oldest)", 
    y = "Volume of Open Tickets"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold"),
    # Angle the text slightly to ensure all 12 month labels fit cleanly
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

@fig-robust-binning demonstrates that the peaks at 60 and 170 days are stable and not binning artifacts. However, because this observation still relies on visual inspection, we must apply a formal statistical test to mathematically confirm their presence.

Hartigan's Dip Test is a non-parametric method designed to detect multimodality [@hartigan1985dip]. The null hypothesis ($H_0$) assumes the distribution is unimodal. Mathematically, it calculates the "dip" statistic ($D$), which represents the maximum vertical distance between the empirical distribution function, $F_n(x)$, and the best-fitting unimodal distribution function, $U(x)$:
$$D = \sup_x \vert{}F_n(x) - U(x)\vert{}$$
If the data contains multiple modes (such as the 60-day and 170-day peaks), $F_n(x)$ will deviate from any fitted unimodal curve. This deviation yields a $p$-value approaching zero, rejecting the null hypothesis.


```{r}
#| label: hartigans-dip-test
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hold

library(diptest)
library(dplyr)

# Test on the continuous days open variable
dip_result <- dip.test(boston_open$days_open_at_yearend)
# Extract and format the results
dip_stat <- round(dip_result$statistic, 4)
dip_pval <- format(dip_result$p.value, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)
# Consolidate output into a single string
conclusion_text <- if(dip_result$p.value < 0.05) {
  "Conclusion: The p-value approaches zero, mathematically rejecting unimodality.\nThe distinct waves in the backlog are structural realities, not binning artifacts."
} else {
  "Conclusion: Failed to reject unimodality."
}

final_output <- paste0(
  "--- Hartigan's Dip Test for Unimodality ---\n",
  "Dip Statistic (D): ", dip_stat, "\n",
  "P-Value:           ", dip_pval, "\n\n",
  conclusion_text, "\n"
)
cat(final_output)
```


Having established the stability of the 60-day and 170-day peaks, we investigate their potential origins by examining monthly requests that are still open at the end of 2024 by department in @fig-open-tickets-by-month.

```{r}
#| label: fig-open-tickets-by-month
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Visualization of departments contributions to open requests at the end of 2024 by starting month (Note that the month order is the reverse of that in @fig-robust-binning (c))."

# Identify the top 4 departments with the most open tickets
top_open_subjects <- boston_open %>%
  count(subject, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 4) %>%
  pull(subject)
# Group the data for the stacked visualization
plot_data_open <- boston_open %>%
  mutate(
    subject_grouped = ifelse(subject %in% top_open_subjects, subject, "All Other Departments"),
    # Factor to ensure the grey baseline sits at the bottom of the stack
    subject_grouped = factor(subject_grouped, levels = c("All Other Departments", top_open_subjects))
  )
# Generate the bar chart
ggplot(plot_data_open, aes(x = open_month, fill = subject_grouped)) +
  geom_bar(color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "All Other Departments" = "grey80",
      # Using a clear, distinct color palette for the top culprits
      setNames(c("#E41A1C", "#377EB8", "#4DAF4A", "#984EA3"), top_open_subjects)
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Year-End Backlog by Month of Origin",
    subtitle = "Exploratory view: Identifying seasonal waves and departmental bottlenecks.",
    x = "Month Ticket Was Opened",
    y = "Volume of Open Tickets at Year-End",
    fill = "Department"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9)
  ) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(ncol = 2, reverse = TRUE))
```

The visualization isolates the source of the 170-day peak: the Transportation - Traffic Division backlog increased sharply in June 2024 and remained elevated.

This increase coincides with the *Sumner Tunnel Restoration Project*. MassDOT executed a full 24/7 closure from July 5 to August 5, 2024, with June dedicated to logistical preparation—altering traffic patterns, setting detours, and modifying transit routes. This shift exceeded the Traffic Division's baseline capacity, creating a localized backlog that persisted through year-end.

Beyond the June peak, the visualization reveals a secondary accumulation originating in October (the ~60-day backlog). Rather than a broad seasonal trend, this was a second, distinct disruption localized to the same department.

In October 2024, the MBTA executed a multi-week *shutdown of the Orange Line subway*, replacing trains with surface-level shuttle buses. To accommodate this, the Traffic Division implemented significant street-level modifications across the southwest corridor, including removing parking spaces, creating temporary bus lanes, and altering traffic flow.

Like the summer closure, this logistical pivot constrained the division's capacity. Routine neighborhood work orders were likely deferred to manage the transit disruption, resulting in a secondary backlog just before the close of the calendar year.

## 2.3 Right-Skewed Distributions: Defining Resolution Metrics

Evaluating service resolution times using the arithmetic mean can misrepresent standard operational performance. Maintenance completion times are rarely normally distributed; instead, they typically exhibit a right skew. The majority of tasks are triaged and closed quickly, while a long tail of complex, disputed, or delayed outliers remains open for months.

This long tail shifts the mean upward, distorting the operational baseline. Consequently, the median provides a more robust central tendency metric for evaluating typical performance and establishing Service Level Agreements (SLAs).

```{r}
#| label: fig-resolution-density-log
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Density of Maintenance Resolution Times (Log Scale)"

library(scales) 

# Summary stats 
res_summary <- boston_clean %>%
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(resolution_days, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median = median(resolution_days, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
ggplot(boston_clean, aes(x = resolution_days)) +
  geom_density(fill = "steelblue", color = "darkblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = res_summary$Mean, color = "darkred", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = res_summary$Median, color = "black", linetype = "solid", linewidth = 1) +
  # log1p transformation safely handles 0-day resolutions
  scale_x_continuous(
    trans = "log1p",
    breaks = c(0, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100, 365),
    labels = label_comma()
  ) +
  # Setting y = Inf and adjusting vjust pins the labels to the top of the plot
  annotate("text", x = res_summary$Mean, y = Inf, 
           label = paste("Mean:\n", round(res_summary$Mean, 1), "days"), 
           color = "darkred", hjust = -0.2, vjust = 1.5, size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = res_summary$Median, y = Inf, 
           label = paste("Median:\n", round(res_summary$Median, 1), "days"), 
           color = "black", hjust = 1.2, vjust = 1.5, size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Density of Maintenance Resolution Times (Log Scale)",
    subtitle = "A log1p scale stretches the immediate closures while revealing the true span of the multi-month right tail.",
    x = "Days to Close (Log Scale)",
    y = "Density of Work Orders"
  )
```

As @fig-resolution-density-log illustrates, even after applying a logarithmic transformation, the distribution remains right-skewed and multi-modal. Because the data does not approximate log-normality, standard parametric statistical models (which assume normally distributed errors) are inappropriate for these data. This distributional shape necessitates the non-parametric and survival-based methodologies applied in subsequent sections.

## 2.4 Isolating Factors of Delay
To identify the variables associated with operational bottlenecks, we first establish a baseline for expected performance. In municipal and property maintenance contexts, this baseline is defined by a *Service Level Agreement (SLA)*—a standardized target time for resolving a specific request type.

Absolute resolution times lack relative context, and evaluating tickets on a binary "pass/fail" basis discards valuable variance. Instead, we calculate the *SLA Delta* (signed delay) for every closed ticket: the Actual Resolution Time minus the SLA Target Time.

> **Methodological Note:** We measure delay in absolute time (raw days) rather than a relative percentage (SLA Delta / SLA Duration) because workforce capacity constraints and operational impacts scale in days, rather than administrative ratios. Additionally, emergency triage tasks frequently have same-day SLAs (zero-day durations), which would yield mathematically undefined values if a ratio were applied.

By analyzing the continuous distribution of this SLA Delta across the dataset, we can evaluate which specific variables are most associated with extended delays.

### 2.4.1 The SLA Delta Distribution

We first analyze the overall distribution of the SLA Delta. A value of $0$ indicates the ticket was closed exactly on the deadline. Negative values represent early closures, while positive values quantify the extent to which a ticket was overdue.

```{r}
#| label: fig-sla-delta-distribution
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of SLA Delta."

# Calculate the exact delta in days
sla_delta_data <- boston_clean %>%
  filter(!is.na(sla_target_dt), subject != "Animal Control") %>%
  mutate(
    sla_delta_days = as.numeric(difftime(closed_dt, sla_target_dt, units = "days")),
    # Categorize for the plot fill
    compliance_status = ifelse(sla_delta_days <= 0, "On Time (Early)", "Overdue (Late)")
  )
# Plot the distribution of the delta
ggplot(sla_delta_data, aes(x = sla_delta_days, fill = compliance_status)) +
  # boundary = 0 added here to prevent overlapping bins at zero
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = 0, color = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  # Add the hard SLA deadline reference line
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "black", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("On Time (Early)" = "steelblue", "Overdue (Late)" = "darkred")) +
  # Zoom the x-axis to a relevant operational window (e.g., 30 days early to 30 days late)
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-30, 30)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of SLA Delta",
    subtitle = "The variance of actual closure times relative to their expected deadlines.",
    x = "SLA Delta (Days)",
    y = "Volume of Work Orders",
    fill = "Status"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

This continuous distribution reveals the variance and clustering relative to the deadline. @fig-sla-delta-distribution shows a pronounced concentration of work orders closed immediately prior to the deadline, a sharp drop-off at zero, and a right-skewed tail of overdue tickets.

### 2.4.2 Factors Associated with Resolution Variance

To identify variables associated with early or delayed closures, we test the relationship between the available categorical features (e.g., department, queue, geography) and the continuous SLA Delta.Given the prevalence of outliers, traditional parametric methods (such as ANOVA) are statistically inappropriate. 

Furthermore, the large sample size ($N$) causes standard $p$-values to approach zero even for negligible differences, while the heavy right skew violates the underlying assumptions of Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression, rendering variance explained ($R^2$) metrics unreliable.

#### Volume-Weighted K-S Distance

o robustly evaluate categorical differences without relying on variance, we compare the *Empirical Cumulative Distribution Functions (ECDFs)* using a volume-weighted *Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) statistic*.

Let $F_{global}(x)$ represent the ECDF of the SLA Delta for the entire dataset. For any given categorical factor (e.g., `department`) partitioned into $K$ subgroups, let $F_k(x)$ represent the ECDF for a specific subgroup $k$.

The standard K-S statistic, $D_k$, measures the maximum absolute vertical distance between the subgroup's ECDF and the global ECDF:

$$D_k = \sup_x |F_k(x) - F_{global}(x)|$$

This yields a value bounded between $0$ (identical distributions) and $1$ (no distributional overlap). Because the K-S test evaluates empirical percentiles rather than mean variance, it is a non-parametric statistic and is therefore robust to outliers.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ks-statistic-explanation
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Graphical explanation of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic."
# 1. Identify a "Goldilocks" subgroup (high volume, moderate D_k around 0.35)
global_dist <- sla_delta_data$sla_delta_days

illustrative_group <- sla_delta_data %>%
  group_by(type) %>%
  filter(n() > 5000) %>% 
  summarise(
    ks_stat = suppressWarnings(ks.test(sla_delta_days, global_dist)$statistic),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(diff_from_target = abs(ks_stat - 0.35)) %>%
  arrange(diff_from_target) %>%
  slice(1)

max_type_name <- illustrative_group$type
max_type_dist <- sla_delta_data %>% filter(type == max_type_name) %>% pull(sla_delta_days)

# 2. Calculate the exact point of maximum vertical distance
x_vals <- sort(unique(c(global_dist, max_type_dist)))
ecdf_global_vals <- ecdf(global_dist)(x_vals)
ecdf_max_vals <- ecdf(max_type_dist)(x_vals)

diffs <- abs(ecdf_global_vals - ecdf_max_vals)
max_idx <- which.max(diffs)

x_max_diff <- x_vals[max_idx]
y_global <- ecdf_global_vals[max_idx]
y_max <- ecdf_max_vals[max_idx]
max_d_stat <- diffs[max_idx]

# Define dynamic labels to map math notation to the data
global_label <- "F_global : Global Baseline"
subgroup_label <- paste0("F_k : '", max_type_name, "' (Factor: type)")

# 3. Create the dataset for plotting
plot_data <- sla_delta_data %>%
  mutate(Curve = global_label) %>%
  bind_rows(
    sla_delta_data %>%
      filter(type == max_type_name) %>%
      mutate(Curve = subgroup_label)
  )

# 4. Generate the explanatory plot
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = sla_delta_days, color = Curve)) +
  stat_ecdf(linewidth = 1) +
  # Add the vertical segment illustrating D_k
  annotate("segment", x = x_max_diff, xend = x_max_diff,
           y = y_global, yend = y_max,
           color = "darkred", linewidth = 1.2, 
           arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.1, "inches"))) +
  # Annotate the exact D_k value mathematically
  annotate("text", x = x_max_diff + 2, y = mean(c(y_global, y_max)),
           label = paste0("D[k] == ", round(max_d_stat, 3)), parse = TRUE,
           color = "darkred", hjust = 0, size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  # Reference line for the SLA deadline (0 days)
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "black", linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.5) +
  # Map colors directly to the new dynamic labels
  scale_color_manual(values = setNames(c("darkgray", "steelblue"), c(global_label, subgroup_label))) +
  # Lock the zoom back to the critical operational window
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-30, 30)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Visualizing the Kolmogorov-Smirnov Statistic",
    subtitle = "The D_k statistic represents the maximum absolute vertical distance between the global distribution\nand a specific subgroup (in this example, the 'Parking Enforcement' level of the 'type' factor).",
    x = "SLA Delta (Days)",
    y = "Cumulative Proportion of Tickets Closed",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold")
  )
```

#### Results: The Dominance of Organizational Routing

To evaluate the overall explanatory power of a categorical factor, we aggregate the $D_k$ scores across all its subgroups. Taking a simple average would artificially inflate the influence of subgroups with very low ticket volumes. Therefore, we calculate the Volume-Weighted K-S Score ($D_{weighted}$) by weighting each subgroup's K-S statistic by its proportional ticket volume:

$$D_{weighted} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \left( \frac{n_k}{N} \right) D_k$$

Where $n_k$ is the number of work orders in subgroup $k$, and $N$ is the total volume across all subgroups. This weighting ensures the final metric reflects operational scale, dampening variance from small subgroups while capturing deviations in high-volume queues.

```{r}
#| label: feature-dependency-ks
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

# Global baseline distribution
global_dist <- sla_delta_data$sla_delta_days
total_n <- nrow(sla_delta_data)
factors_to_test <- c("subject", "reason", "type", "queue", "department", 
                     "fire_district", "pwd_district", "city_council_district", 
                     "police_district", "neighborhood", "neighborhood_services_district", 
                     "ward", "precinct", "location_zipcode", "source")
# Function to calculate the Weighted K-S Distance and extract p-values
calc_weighted_ks <- function(factor_name, data, global_dist, total_n) {
  data %>%
    group_split(!!sym(factor_name)) %>%
    map_dfr(function(df) {
      level_dist <- df$sla_delta_days
      level_n <- nrow(df)
      # Skip virtually empty levels to prevent test errors
      if(level_n < 5) return(tibble(level_n = level_n, ks_stat = 0, p_val = 1))
      # Suppress warnings for expected ties
      ks_res <- suppressWarnings(ks.test(level_dist, global_dist))
      tibble(
        level_n = level_n,
        ks_stat = ks_res$statistic,
        p_val = ks_res$p.value
      )
    }) %>%
    summarise(
      Factor = factor_name,
      Weighted_KS_Score = sum(ks_stat * (level_n / total_n)),
      Median_P_Value = median(p_val)
    )
}
# Map across all factors and rank
ks_results <- map_dfr(factors_to_test, ~calc_weighted_ks(.x, sla_delta_data, global_dist, total_n)) %>%
  arrange(desc(Weighted_KS_Score)) %>%
  mutate(
    Weighted_KS_Score = round(Weighted_KS_Score, 4),
    Median_P_Value = format(Median_P_Value, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)
  )
```

Applying this non-parametric ranking to all organizational, task-based, and geographic features reveals a clear hierarchy of variance drivers displayed in @tbl-factor-ranking.


```{r}
#| label: tbl-factor-ranking
#| tbl-cap: "Factor Dependency Ranking (Weighted K-S Distance)"
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

library(knitr)

# Generate the formal Quarto table from the previous ks_results tibble
kable(
  ks_results, 
  col.names = c("Factor", "Weighted K-S Score", "Median P-Value"),
  align = c('l', 'c', 'c')
)
```

Applying this non-parametric ranking to all organizational, task-based, and geographic features reveals the hierarchy of variance drivers displayed in @tbl-factor-ranking.

As the table illustrates, a distinct structural divide emerges: factors governing "what the work is and who does it" account for the highest variance, while factors dictating "where the work is" rank at the bottom.

To clearly visualize this distinction, we grouped these features into two primary categories—Organizational & Task Routing versus Geographic Boundaries—and plotted their K-S effect sizes in @fig-factor-ranking-lollipop.

```{r}
#| label: fig-factor-ranking-lollipop
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Visualizing the K-S Ranking: Organizational variables fundamentally drive SLA variance, while flat geographic boundaries provide minimal predictive signal."

library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

# Categorize the factors and clean names for the plot
plot_ks <- ks_results %>%
  mutate(
    # Create the macro-categories based on the table's findings
    Macro_Category = if_else(
      Factor %in% c("subject", "reason", "type", "queue", "department", "source"),
      "Organizational & Task Routing", 
      "Geographic Boundaries"
    ),
    # Clean up the factor names for the y-axis
    Clean_Factor = str_to_title(str_replace_all(Factor, "_", " ")),
    Clean_Factor = fct_reorder(Clean_Factor, Weighted_KS_Score)
  )

ggplot(plot_ks, aes(x = Weighted_KS_Score, y = Clean_Factor, color = Macro_Category)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = Weighted_KS_Score, y = Clean_Factor, yend = Clean_Factor), linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Organizational & Task Routing" = "#d73027", "Geographic Boundaries" = "#4575b4")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "What Drives Service Delays?",
    subtitle = "Organizational routing dominates variance. Geographic bins provide almost no predictive signal.",
    x = "Weighted K-S Score (Distributional Shift)",
    y = NULL,
    color = "Variable Type"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
  )
```

**Task & Organizational Factors**: The variables exhibiting the highest distributional shift (`queue`, `type`, `subject`, and `department`) are organizational and functional. These factors dictate the nature of the physical task and the assigned workforce. Because a task's nature determines its complexity, labor requirements, and necessary equipment, it acts as the primary constraint on the resolution timeline. Geographic location does not alter the physical requirements of the work itself, explaining its minimal impact on timeline variance relative to the global baseline.

**Limitations of Administrative Boundaries**: Spatial features (`precinct`, `ward`, `location_zipcode`, and municipal `district`) cluster at the bottom of the K-S results. This low ranking should not be interpreted as uniform geographic performance. Rather, it demonstrates that partitioning data by large administrative boundaries is an ineffective method for measuring localized service delivery. Categorical bins obscure physical topology by averaging out street-level disparities, as discrete variables lack spatial context regarding neighboring areas. Evaluating continuous spatial relationships requires localized autocorrelation, which is applied in Section 2.9.

### 2.4.3 Result Illustration: Extremes of Organizational Routing

To illustrate the practical impact of the K-S findings, we can evaluate performance across different digital queues.

If organizational factors strongly influence timeline variance, substantial differences should appear between distinct workflows. To examine this, we filtered for high-volume queues (handling over 500 requests) and compared the five queues with the earliest median completion times against the five queues with the most delayed median completion times.


```{r}
#| label: fig-variance-extremes
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Contrasting SLA Delta distributions of the fastest and slowest high-volume queues. The digital routing queue strictly dictates whether a task is systematically early or structurally delayed."

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(forcats)

# 1. Identify the best and worst performing high-volume queues
queue_summary <- sla_delta_data %>%
  group_by(queue) %>%
  summarise(
    total_tickets = n(),
    median_delta = median(sla_delta_days, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  # Isolate only robust, high-volume queues
  filter(total_tickets > 500)

# Extract the names of the top 5 and bottom 5 queues
fastest_queues <- queue_summary %>% slice_min(median_delta, n = 5) %>% pull(queue)
slowest_queues <- queue_summary %>% slice_max(median_delta, n = 5) %>% pull(queue)
target_queues <- c(fastest_queues, slowest_queues)

# 2. Filter the raw data and categorize for plotting
plot_data_extremes <- sla_delta_data %>%
  filter(queue %in% target_queues) %>%
  mutate(
    Performance = if_else(queue %in% fastest_queues, "Systematically Early", "Systematically Delayed"),
    # Reorder the factor based on median delay for a clean visual staircase
    queue = fct_reorder(queue, sla_delta_days, .fun = median, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Calculate dynamic axis limits to ensure all boxes fit (ignoring extreme 5% outliers)
x_lower <- quantile(plot_data_extremes$sla_delta_days, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
x_upper <- quantile(plot_data_extremes$sla_delta_days, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)

# 3. Generate the Boxplot
ggplot(plot_data_extremes, aes(x = sla_delta_days, y = queue, fill = Performance)) +
  # Suppress severe outliers, thicken whiskers (linewidth), and pop the median (fatten)
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8, outlier.alpha = 0.05, outlier.size = 0.5, 
               color = "black", linewidth = 0.6, fatten = 3) +
  # Reference line for the exact deadline
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Use the dynamically calculated limits instead of hardcoded numbers
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(x_lower, x_upper)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Systematically Early" = "#4575b4", "Systematically Delayed" = "#d73027")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "The Operational Divide: Best vs. Worst Queues",
    subtitle = "Visualizing the K-S finding: The assigned digital queue dictates massive timeline variance.",
    x = "SLA Delta (Days)",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Queue Performance"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold")
  )
```

As @fig-variance-extremes (image_c4874d.png) illustrates, the assigned routing queue closely corresponds to the overall lifecycle of a request.

**The early-closing queues (shown in blue)**, such as routine park maintenance and graffiti removal, consistently close well ahead of their target deadlines. 

**Conversely, the delayed queues (shown in red)**, including traffic signal engineering reviews and automated interface queues, exhibit consistent backlogs, with their interquartile ranges falling primarily past the scheduled SLA target.

This comparison demonstrates the operational relevance of the K-S results: organizational routing is a primary driver of SLA timeline variance. Having evaluated categorical dimensions, the analysis next shifts to unstructured text fields, examining technician notes to evaluate whether operational signals exist outside predefined administrative bins.

## 2.5 Text Analytics: Extracting Operational Signals

Unstructured free text (such as technician `closure_reason` notes) may contain operational context absent from categorical variables. Processing these text entries requires *Natural Language Processing (NLP)* techniques. 

We first apply an unsupervised machine learning pipeline to identify broad thematic patterns associated with service delays.

### 2.5.1 Unsupervised Classification

#### 2.5.1.1 Clustering

To categorize the text securely without transmitting data to external APIs, we deployed a locally hosted pipeline utilizing BERTopic [@grootendorst2022] in conjunction with a Hugging Face sentence-transformers embedding model [@reimers2019]. This pipeline converts unstructured text into high-dimensional numerical embeddings, which are subsequently clustered using the HDBSCAN algorithm [@mcinnes2017hdbscan].

Due to the computational demands of Transformer models, the classification script was executed externally in Python. The outputs were saved as a static dataset to ensure efficient document rendering.

Following the clustering phase, we extract the core themes of each group using Class-based Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (c-TF-IDF). Unlike standard TF-IDF, which evaluates individual documents, c-TF-IDF aggregates all entries within a single cluster into one consolidated document. This isolates the distinct keywords that differentiate a specific operational cluster from the overall dataset.

> **Note**: The clustering algorithm assigns a topic ID of -1 to statistical outliers—tickets with highly unique text that do not fit into any broader operational pattern.


```{r}
#| label: fig-plot-bertopic-results
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Volume of SLA breaches categorized by AI-discovered operational themes."

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(here)

# Read ONLY the newly generated AI columns and the Ticket ID
ai_results <- read_csv(here("data", "boston_bertopic_results.csv")) %>%
  select(case_enquiry_id, topic_id, ai_topic_name) 
# Join the AI topics to your existing SLA dataset and filter
ai_plot_data <- sla_delta_data %>%
  inner_join(ai_results, by = "case_enquiry_id") %>%
  filter(compliance_status == "Overdue (Late)", topic_id != -1) %>%
  mutate(
    clean_topic = str_remove(ai_topic_name, "^\\d+_"),
    clean_topic = str_replace_all(clean_topic, "_", " "),
    clean_topic = str_to_title(clean_topic)
  ) %>%
  count(clean_topic, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)
# Generate the visualization
ggplot(ai_plot_data, aes(x = n, y = reorder(clean_topic, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Top Causes of Operational Delays (Discovered via AI)",
    subtitle = "Unsupervised clustering of closure notes reveals distinct systemic bottlenecks.",
    x = "Volume of Delayed Work Orders",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold")
  )
```

#### 2.5.1.2 Refining Labels with Local Generative AI (Ollama)

While the clustering pipeline groups the data using c-TF-IDF keyword strings (e.g., "Related Responds Patrols Encourage"), these raw statistical labels lack operational readability, as illustrated in @fig-raw-clusters.

To translate these machine-readable statistics into interpretable categories, we utilized R's `r "httr"` package to query a locally hosted Llama 3 instance via Ollama [@ollama2024]. This step applies municipal context to synthesize the raw keyword strings into concise operational labels, maintaining data privacy by executing the generative inference entirely on-device.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-llm-topic-translation
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| cache: true
#| tbl-cap: "Automated Topic Translation via Local Llama 3 (Offline API)"

library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(here)
library(knitr)
library(httr)

# CLEAN FIRST, then get the Top 15 Unique topics
ai_results <- read_csv(here("data", "boston_bertopic_results.csv"))
topic_summary <- ai_results %>%
  filter(topic_id != -1) %>%
  mutate(
    clean_raw_topic = str_remove(ai_topic_name, "^\\d+_"),
    clean_raw_topic = str_replace_all(clean_raw_topic, "_", " ")
  ) %>%
  count(clean_raw_topic, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)
# Direct Local API with the Proper Persona
translate_topic <- function(messy_string) {
  sys_prompt <- "You are an expert municipal data analyst for the City of Boston. You classify messy 311 work order keywords."
  user_prompt <- paste0(
    "Translate this messy keyword string into a clean, 3-to-4 word operational category label (e.g., 'Equipment Maintenance', 'Duplicate Request').\n\n",
    "Return ONLY the label. Do not include quotes, formatting, or introductory text.\n\n",
    "Keyword: ", messy_string
  )
  # Send offline request directly to local Mac memory
  res <- tryCatch({
    POST(
      url = "http://localhost:11434/api/generate",
      body = list(
        model = "llama3",
        prompt = user_prompt,
        system = sys_prompt,
        stream = FALSE
      ),
      encode = "json",
      timeout(30)
    )
  }, error = function(e) return(NULL))
  if (is.null(res) || status_code(res) != 200) return("API Connection Failed")
  raw_text <- content(res, as = "parsed", type = "application/json")$response
  # Strip out any markdown or quotes the LLM tries to sneak in
  clean_label <- str_remove_all(raw_text, '["*]') %>% str_trim()
  return(as.character(clean_label))
}
# Loop through the 15 topics
llm_clean_names <- map_chr(topic_summary$clean_raw_topic, translate_topic)
# Build and print the crosswalk table
topic_crosswalk <- tibble(
  `Original c-TF-IDF String` = topic_summary$clean_raw_topic,
  `LLM Dashboard Label` = llm_clean_names
)
kable(topic_crosswalk, caption = "Automated Topic Translation via Local Llama 3 (Offline API)")
```

With the statistical keywords mapped to operational labels (@tbl-translation, image_c559df.png), we update the visualization to examine the distribution of delayed work orders in @fig-translated-clusters.

```{r}
#| label: fig-plot-bertopic-results-after-ollama
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Volume of SLA breaches categorized by human-readable operational themes."

# Re-isolate the delayed tickets and format the topic strings to match the crosswalk
ai_plot_data_translated <- sla_delta_data %>%
  inner_join(ai_results, by = "case_enquiry_id") %>%
  filter(compliance_status == "Overdue (Late)", topic_id != -1) %>%
  mutate(
    clean_raw_topic = str_remove(ai_topic_name, "^\\d+_"),
    clean_raw_topic = str_replace_all(clean_raw_topic, "_", " ")
  ) %>%
  count(clean_raw_topic, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  # Join the translated labels generated by Ollama
  left_join(topic_crosswalk, by = c("clean_raw_topic" = "Original c-TF-IDF String")) %>%
  # Fallback to Title Case just in case a delayed topic wasn't in the global Top 15
  mutate(
    final_label = ifelse(is.na(`LLM Dashboard Label`), str_to_title(clean_raw_topic), `LLM Dashboard Label`)
  )

# Generate the updated visualization
ggplot(ai_plot_data_translated, aes(x = n, y = reorder(final_label, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", color = "white", alpha = 0.9) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Top Causes of Operational Delays (Translated via AI)",
    subtitle = "Unsupervised clustering of closure notes, categorized by local Llama 3.",
    x = "Volume of Delayed Work Orders",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold")
  )
```

#### 2.5.1.3 Validation via Departmental Enrichment

Using the synthesized operational labels, we evaluate how these unsupervised clusters map to existing municipal departments to validate the accuracy of the NLP pipeline.

By calculating *Standardized Pearson Residuals* from a *Chi-Square test*, the heatmap in @fig-topic-factor-enrichment identifies which text topics are statistically over-represented in specific departments.

```{r}
#| label: fig-topic-factor-enrichment
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Enrichment heatmap showing which AI topics are statistically over-represented across municipal departments. Department abbreviations: BTDT (Transportation), INFO (Mayor's Hotline), ISD (Inspectional Services), PARK (Parks & Recreation), PROP (Property Management), PWDx (Public Works)."

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(here)

# Load the AI results and join the LLM translated labels
ai_df <- read_csv(here("data", "boston_bertopic_results.csv")) %>%
  filter(topic_id != -1, !is.na(department)) %>%
  mutate(
    clean_raw_topic = str_remove(ai_topic_name, "^\\d+_"),
    clean_raw_topic = str_replace_all(clean_raw_topic, "_", " ")
  ) %>%
  # Bring in the translations from the previous chunk
  left_join(topic_crosswalk, by = c("clean_raw_topic" = "Original c-TF-IDF String")) %>%
  mutate(
    # Fallback to the title-cased raw topic if it wasn't in our Top 15 translated list
    Final_Label = ifelse(is.na(`LLM Dashboard Label`), str_to_title(clean_raw_topic), `LLM Dashboard Label`)
  )
# Focus on top departments and top topics to keep the grid readable
top_depts  <- ai_df %>% count(department, sort = TRUE) %>% slice_head(n = 6) %>% pull(department)
top_topics <- ai_df %>% count(Final_Label, sort = TRUE) %>% slice_head(n = 12) %>% pull(Final_Label)
filtered_df <- ai_df %>%
  filter(department %in% top_depts, Final_Label %in% top_topics)
# Create a contingency table and run Chi-Square to get Standardized Residuals
contingency_matrix <- table(filtered_df$Final_Label, filtered_df$department)
chisq_res <- chisq.test(contingency_matrix)
# Convert residuals back to a tidy dataframe for ggplot
enrichment_data <- as.data.frame(chisq_res$stdres) %>%
  rename(Topic = Var1, Department = Var2, StdResidual = Freq)
# Visualize as an Enrichment Heatmap using the clean LLM labels
ggplot(enrichment_data, aes(x = Department, y = Topic, fill = StdResidual)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2b83ba", mid = "#ffffbf", high = "#d7191c",
    midpoint = 0,
    name = "Standardized\nResidual"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Enrichment of AI Topics Across Departments",
    subtitle = "Red indicates strong over-representation (residual > +2); Blue indicates under-representation.",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold")
  )
```

The results demonstrate expected organizational alignment. For example, "Tree Pruning Maintenance" is strongly associated with the Parks Department (`PARK`), while "Cart Maintenance" aligns with Public Works (`PWDX`). Additionally, "Customer Feedback" corresponds with the Mayor's Hotline (`INFO`). Rather than revealing novel operational insights, these predictable associations serve as a validation step. They confirm that the unsupervised model successfully extracted accurate, department-specific themes directly from the unstructured text, verifying the pipeline's reliability for potential downstream use of these clusters.

### 2.5.2 Structural Vocabulary Extraction

While topic modeling provided unsupervised insights, municipal data is inherently structured around strict administrative categories (e.g., `department`, `queue`, `neighborhood`). To map the specific vocabulary associated with these categories, we implemented an information-theoretic pipeline.

#### 2.5.2.1 The EMI and PMI Mathematical Framework

**Addressing Context Limits via Semantic Representation**

While *Large Language Models (LLMs)* can synthesize text, processing a category's entire work history (often exceeding 50,000 raw tickets) is computationally prohibitive and exceeds standard context windows.

Conversely, relying on random sampling introduces representational bias: high-volume, repetitive tasks (e.g., daily trash removal) overshadow specialized, lower-volume technical work (e.g., electrical infrastructure), yielding an incomplete vocabulary profile.

To address this, we apply *Expected* and *Pointwise Mutual Information (EMI/PMI)*. Rather than sampling raw tickets, this approach transforms unstructured closure notes into a weighted array of high-signal tokens, isolating the structural vocabulary associated with a given category.

**Expected Mutual Information (EMI)**

Before evaluating category-specific vocabulary, we filter out administrative noise. Terms such as "completed," "resident," or "arrived" appear uniformly across categories and offer minimal structural signal. To identify and remove these terms, we calculate Expected Mutual Information (EMI). This metric aggregates a word's ($w$) probability distribution across all categories ($c \in C$) to quantify its overall informational value:
$$EMI(w) = \sum_{c \in C} P(c \vert{} w) \cdot \log_2 \left( \frac{P(w, c)}{P(w)P(c)} \right)$$
Words yielding $EMI \le 0$ provide no structural information and are removed from the global vocabulary. This filtering reduces the free text to a core vocabulary of operational terms.

**Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI)**

Following the EMI filtering, we use Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) to measure the association between a specific word ($w$) and a specific category ($c$). PMI compares the joint probability of the word and category against the probability of their independent occurrences:
$$PMI(w, c) = \log_2 \left( \frac{P(w, c)}{P(w)P(c)} \right)$$

* $PMI > 0$: The word co-occurs with the category more frequently than expected by chance (Attraction).

* $PMI = 0$: The word's occurrence is independent of the category (Independence).

* $PMI < 0$: The word co-occurs with the category less frequently than expected by chance (Repulsion).

In summary, the raw text is first filtered for high-signal words using EMI, and PMI is subsequently applied to isolate the vocabulary associated with a specific category. This two-step approach is applied below to the `department` variable, evaluating its $\vert{}C\vert{}=19$ distinct organizational categories.

#### 2.5.2.2 Categorical Feature Selection

Prior to applying the mutual information framework, the dataset's categorical variables were evaluated to exclude features that introduce target leakage or hyper-granularity (which fragments the probability distribution).

@tbl-retained-factors and @tbl-excluded-factors detail the inclusion and exclusion criteria applied to define the final categorical set ($C$) for the EMI pipeline.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-retained-factors
#| tbl-cap: "Retained Analytical Factors (Independent Variables)"
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

library(tibble)
library(knitr)

retained_factors <- tribble(
  ~`Categorical Factor`, ~`Unique Levels`, ~`Analytical Purpose`,
  "`source`", "6", "Evaluates if constituent intake channels (e.g., App vs. Call Center) generate distinct linguistic patterns.",
  "`subject`", "10", "The highest-level macro-routing bucket.",
  "`department`", "19", "Maps the core operational vocabulary of distinct municipal workforces.",
  "`neighborhood`", "24", "Retained as a control factor to test if vocabulary changes geographically.",
  "`reason`", "45", "Mid-level operational classification.",
  "`type`", "173", "High-granularity operational classification.",
  "`queue`", "187", "The exact digital routing destination. Expected to yield the highest-fidelity PMI signals."
)

kable(retained_factors, align = c('l', 'c', 'l'))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-excluded-factors
#| tbl-cap: "Excluded Variables & Justification"
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

library(tibble)
library(knitr)

excluded_factors <- tribble(
  ~`Excluded Variable`, ~`Levels`, ~`Primary Justification for Exclusion`,
  "`submitted_photo`", "1", "**Zero Variance.** Cannot be used to calculate a probability distribution.",
  "`on_time`, `case_status`", "2", "**Target Leakage / Scope.** We are mapping organizational topology, not SLA compliance metrics.",
  "`case_title`", "3,753", "**Secondary Text.** Functions as a free-text field rather than a categorical grouping structure.",
  "`precinct`, `ward`, `location_zipcode`", "37 - 255", "**Geographic Redundancy.** `neighborhood` is retained as the geographic control; finer administrative bins fracture the baseline probabilities.",
  "`case_enquiry_id`, `location_street_name`, `geom_4326`, `location`", "73K - 282K", "**Hyper-Granular Identifiers.** Unique row identifiers and precise coordinates fragment the denominator, causing the MI log-ratio to explode into statistical noise.",
  "`open_dt`, `closed_dt`, `sla_target_dt`, `longitude`, `latitude`", "Continuous", "**Continuous Time & Space.** Cannot be passed into categorical mutual information models without arbitrary temporal or spatial binning."
)

kable(excluded_factors, align = c('l', 'c', 'l'))
```

# Workflow Tracking:

source("../R/pointwise_mutual_information.R") # (Department-specific PMI mapping)
