```{r}
#| label: fig-emi-distribution
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of Expected Mutual Information (EMI) word counts, with factors ordered from top-left to bottom-right by decreasing mean EMI."

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(scales)
library(readr)

mi_results <- read_csv("../data/mi_results.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# 1. Calculate mean Expected MI per factor to establish a decreasing sort order
factor_ranking <- mi_results %>%
  group_by(factor) %>%
  summarise(mean_emi = mean(expected_mi, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_emi)) %>%
  pull(factor)

# 2. Create the "Global" summary pseudo-factor (Max EMI across all factors for each word)
global_mi <- mi_results %>%
  group_by(word) %>%
  summarise(expected_mi = max(expected_mi, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(factor = "Global (Max EMI)")

# 3. Combine data and set factor levels: Global first, followed by factors ordered by mean EMI
plot_data <- bind_rows(global_mi, mi_results) %>%
  mutate(factor = factor(factor, levels = c("Global (Max EMI)", factor_ranking)))

# 4. Generate the 4x2 faceted plot
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = expected_mi, fill = factor)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, color = "black", linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ factor, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  # Log-transform the X-axis to spread out the dense region near zero
  scale_x_continuous(
    trans = "log1p",
    breaks = c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2),
    labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.01)
  ) +
  # Log-transform the Y-axis counts
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = scales::comma,
    breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title = "The Signal Filter: Expected Mutual Information Distribution",
    subtitle = "Factors ordered by decreasing mean Expected MI, highlighting structural information density.",
    x = "Expected Mutual Information (log1p bits)",
    y = "Number of Words (log scale)",
    fill = "Factor"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "grey30"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```


#### 2.5.2.3 Global Signal & Functional Alignment

Applying the Expected Mutual Information (EMI) equation across the structural categories yields the distribution in @fig-emi-distribution. Plotted on a logarithmic scale, the density near zero indicates that the majority of tokens are administrative noise distributed almost evenly across all categories.

In contrast, the long right tail represents the structural vocabulary that passed the $EMI > 0$ threshold with *high* information scores.

Furthermore, ranking these factors by mean EMI reveals an alignment between vocabulary density and operational function.

The factors with the highest mean EMI (`queue`, `type`, `reason`, `department`) are strictly functional. These variables dictate the nature of the physical task and the assigned workforce. Because the nature of the task determines the required tools and statuses, it also defines the operational vocabulary.

In contrast, circumstantial variables like `neighborhood` and `source` do not alter the physical requirements of the work, yielding a correspondingly low semantic footprint.

This finding corroborates the SLA variance results established via K-S testing in Section 2.4. The functional categories that govern the physical complexity of the work—and thereby influence the SLA timeline—are the same categories that exhibit the highest structural vocabulary mean EMI.

> **Note**: Using the mean EMI rather than the median EMI is better here, as it emphasizes the contribution of large EMI values.

#### 2.5.2.4 High-Signal Vocabulary by Department

Applying the mutual information framework across the 19 departments isolates the top 200 highest-signal words for each department.

The interactive table below displays these terms, ranked by their Normalized Pointwise Mutual Information (NPMI) score. Words appearing at the top of a department's column are strongly associated with that specific workforce, indicating the physical tasks, equipment, and administrative shorthand that characterize their operations.

While automated summarization of these vocabularies is explored in subsequent sections, direct human inspection of the raw PMI rankings is highly effective for theme identification. Simply reviewing the top terms in each column reveals cohesive operational clusters—such as pest control ("burrows", "baiting", "droppings") in Inspectional Services (`ISD`) or arboreal maintenance ("forestry", "canopy", "replant") in Parks and Recreation (`PARK`). Because automated generative models can introduce stochastic variability, this deterministic matrix serves as a robust, standalone tool for operational discovery.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pmi-departments
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(DT)
library(tibble)

# 1. Map short codes to full department names
dept_mapping <- tribble(
  ~code, ~full_name,
  "PWDx", "Public Works",
  "BTDT", "Transportation",
  "PARK", "Parks and Recreation",
  "ISD", "Inspectional Services",
  "GEN_", "General / 311",
  "BWSC", "Water and Sewer",
  "INFO", "Info / Hotline",
  "ANML", "Animal Control",
  "PROP", "Property Management",
  "BPD_", "Police Department",
  "DISB", "Disabilities Commission",
  "DND_", "Neighborhood Development",
  "ONS_", "Neighborhood Services"
)

# Load the wide-format PMI data
pmi_wide <- read_csv("../data/department_all19_pmi_excel.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Clean the dataframe for HTML display
pmi_display <- pmi_wide %>%
  select(ends_with("_word")) %>%
  rename_with(~ sub("_word$", "", .x))

# Rename the columns to include full names based on the mapping
new_col_names <- sapply(names(pmi_display), function(col) {
  full_name <- dept_mapping$full_name[dept_mapping$code == col]
  if (length(full_name) > 0) paste0(col, " (", full_name, ")") else col
})
names(pmi_display) <- new_col_names

pmi_display <- pmi_display %>% mutate(Rank = row_number(), .before = 1)

# Generate the interactive DataTable
datatable(
  pmi_display,
  rownames = FALSE, 
  class = 'display compact', 
  caption = "Top 200 Operational Words by Department (Ranked by NPMI, Tie-broken by Volume)",
  options = list(
    pageLength = 20,       
    scrollX = TRUE,        
    scrollY = "680px",     
    dom = 'ftip',          
    searchHighlight = TRUE 
  )
) %>%
  formatStyle(columns = names(pmi_display), fontSize = '13px')
```

#### 2.5.2.5 Vocabulary Interpretation via Local Generative AI

To provide an interpretable view of the extracted vocabulary, we integrated a local Large Language Model (LLM) into the pipeline.

Rather than processing raw operational tickets—an approach limited by context windows and noise—the LLM was restricted to the top 200 high-signal words isolated by the PMI algorithm, functioning strictly as a semantic translator. The model was initialized with a structured prompt defining its analytical role:

> **Prompt** "You are a municipal operations analyst. I am providing you with a list of the top statistically significant words extracted from the 'closure notes' of a specific city department, sorted by their Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) score. This means these words represent the highly specific, unique physical tasks and vocabulary of this department.
Based only on these words, write a concise, 3-sentence operational profile describing exactly what this department does in the physical world. Do not invent tasks outside of this vocabulary." 

Descriptions provided by the LLM are presented in @tbl-llm-profiles.

> **Note**: The Boston Police Department (BPD) profile generated below relies heavily on words related to noise and public disturbances. This is because the 311 system is explicitly reserved for non-emergency municipal issues; active crimes are routed through 911 and therefore do not appear in this dataset's vocabulary.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-llm-profiles
#| tbl-cap: "Generative Translation of PMI Vocabulary Arrays into Operational Profiles"
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
library(tibble)

# 1. Map short codes to full department names
dept_mapping <- tribble(
  ~code, ~full_name,
  "PWDx", "Public Works",
  "BTDT", "Transportation",
  "PARK", "Parks and Recreation",
  "ISD", "Inspectional Services",
  "GEN_", "General / 311",
  "BWSC", "Water and Sewer",
  "INFO", "Info / Hotline",
  "ANML", "Animal Control",
  "PROP", "Property Management",
  "BPD_", "Police Department",
  "DISB", "Disabilities Commission",
  "DND_", "Neighborhood Development",
  "ONS_", "Neighborhood Services"
)

# Load the LLM-generated profiles and raw PMI results
llm_profiles <- read_csv("../data/department_profiles_llm.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
pmi_raw <- read_csv("../data/pmi_results.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# 2. Calculate Vocab Volume and Median NPMI for the exact array fed to the LLM
metrics_df <- pmi_raw %>%
  filter(factor == "department", pmi > 0) %>%
  group_by(level) %>%
  arrange(desc(scaled_pmi), desc(n_wc)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 200) %>%
  # Count the surviving words and calculate the median
  summarise(
    vocab_size = n(),
    median_npmi = sprintf("%.2f", median(scaled_pmi)), 
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# 3. Clean and format for display
display_profiles <- llm_profiles %>%
  filter(!grepl("Insufficient vocabulary", operational_profile, ignore.case = TRUE)) %>%
  left_join(dept_mapping, by = c("department" = "code")) %>%
  # Join the calculated metrics
  left_join(metrics_df, by = c("department" = "level")) %>%
  mutate(
    Department = paste0(
      "<b>", department, "</b><br>",
      "<span style='font-size:0.85em; color:gray;'>", 
      full_name, "<br>Words: ", vocab_size, " | Med NPMI: ", median_npmi, 
      "</span>"
    )
  ) %>%
  select(Department, `AI-Translated Operational Profile` = operational_profile)

# 4. Render a styled HTML table
kable(display_profiles, format = "html", escape = FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  column_spec(1, width = "20%") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "80%")
```

Operating on the concise arrays generated by the EMI/PMI approach, the LLM produces targeted summaries of each department's operational footprint.

This EMI/PMI/LLM framework can be generalized to any partitioning of the dataset. For example, within property management or service request analytics, this pipeline can automatically characterize specific property groups or maintenance technician clusters.

However, this approach remains susceptible to over-interpretation when applied without *strict constraints*. As observed in certain outputs—such as misinterpreting the Mayor's Hotline (INFO) as a wildlife rescue agency due to terms like "shelter" or "quarantine"—unconstrained language models can confabulate operational scope.

To ensure reliable interpretation, two safeguards must be maintained:

**Sufficient PMI Magnitude**: The PMI scores for the top vocabulary must be high enough, ensuring the model is not parsing low-information noise. In @tbl-pmi-departments, each term is followed by a short representation of its PMI value, the largest possible value being 2.

**Lexical Specificity**: The input vocabulary must be operational and specific. When a department handles administrative workflows rather than distinct physical tasks (such as Neighborhood Development, `DND`, where generic terms like "completed" and "resolved" dominate), the extracted tokens lack the semantic density required for accurate text generation. In such cases, human inspection of the terms and their PMI values is preferable.

## 2.6 Seasonal Demand and System Capacity

To optimize workforce schedules, we must understand seasonal demand fluctuations. High demand alone is not problematic if the workforce is appropriately scaled to handle it.

The true operational insight lies in comparing total inbound ticket volume (Demand) against the volume of missed SLAs (System Failure) month over month. This can reveal the moments when operational capacity is overwhelmed by seasonal surges.

### 2.6.1 Citywide Macro Trends

We first look at the aggregate stress placed on Boston's municipal infrastructure across the entire year.

```{r}
#| label: fig-seasonal-trends-global
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Citywide monthly inbound ticket demand versus the volume of resulting SLA breaches."

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
library(tidyr)
library(scales)

# Base dataset with extracted month
seasonal_base <- sla_delta_data %>%
  mutate(created_month = month(open_dt, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE))
# Global Aggregation
global_summary <- seasonal_base %>%
  group_by(created_month) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Demand = n(),
    SLA_Breaches = sum(compliance_status == "Overdue (Late)", na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Total_Demand, SLA_Breaches),
    names_to = "Metric",
    values_to = "Volume"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Metric = factor(Metric, levels = c("Total_Demand", "SLA_Breaches"), 
                    labels = c("Total Inbound Tickets (Demand)", "Missed SLAs (System Failure)"))
  )
# Build the global seasonal overlay
ggplot(global_summary, aes(x = created_month, y = Volume, group = Metric, color = Metric)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Total Inbound Tickets (Demand)" = "#b3cde3", 
                                "Missed SLAs (System Failure)" = "#e41a1c")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Citywide Seasonal Operational Stress Test",
    subtitle = "Tracking when inbound municipal demand outpaces workforce resolution capacity.",
    x = "Month Request Opened",
    y = "Ticket Volume",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.position = "top",
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

### 2.6.2 Departmental Micro Trends

Because aggregate citywide data might obscure localized bottlenecks, we break this seasonality down by the highest-volume departments (@fig-dept-stress). 

Interestingly, the correlation between demand (blue) and system failure (red) varies significantly by department:

```{r}
#| label: fig-seasonal-trends-department
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Departmental breakdown of monthly demand versus SLA breaches. Department abbreviations: BTDT (Transportation), INFO (Mayor's Hotline), ISD (Inspectional Services), PARK (Parks & Recreation), PROP (Property Management), PWDx (Public Works)."

# Find the top 6 departments by overall ticket volume 
top_depts_season <- seasonal_base %>%
  count(department, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 6) %>%
  pull(department)
# Departmental Aggregation
dept_summary <- seasonal_base %>%
  filter(department %in% top_depts_season) %>%
  group_by(department, created_month) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Demand = n(),
    SLA_Breaches = sum(compliance_status == "Overdue (Late)", na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Total_Demand, SLA_Breaches),
    names_to = "Metric",
    values_to = "Volume"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Metric = factor(Metric, levels = c("Total_Demand", "SLA_Breaches"), 
                    labels = c("Total Inbound Tickets (Demand)", "Missed SLAs (System Failure)"))
  )
# Build the faceted visualization
ggplot(dept_summary, aes(x = created_month, y = Volume, group = Metric, color = Metric)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ department, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Total Inbound Tickets (Demand)" = "#b3cde3", 
                                "Missed SLAs (System Failure)" = "#e41a1c")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Stress Test by Top Departments",
    subtitle = "Comparing capacity thresholds across individual workflows (Note: Y-axes vary by department).",
    x = "Month Request Opened",
    y = "Ticket Volume",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.position = "top",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

**Correlated Capacity Constraints**: For departments like Transportation (`BTDT`), the Mayor's Hotline (`INFO`), and Property Management (`PROP`), missed SLAs closely track inbound volume. When demand spikes, failure rates proportionally rise, indicating rigid capacity constraints where a static workforce cannot absorb the surge.

**Uncorrelated & Elastic Capacity**: Conversely, Parks and Recreation (`PARK`) and Public Works (`PWDx`) demonstrate a decoupled relationship. `PARK`, for example, absorbs a massive summer surge in ticket volume with almost no increase in missed SLAs. This points to highly elastic seasonal scaling, implying that the workforce is appropriately expanded (e.g., via seasonal summer hires) to match the expected environmental demand.

### 2.6.3 Extracting Seasonal Vocabulary Signatures

Initially, we attempted to evaluate temporal shifts by directly feeding raw seasonal ticket data of into unsupervised AI models. However, this direct approach failed to yield meaningful results. Because these algorithms evaluate the entire corpus simultaneously, the baseline administrative noise (e.g., "arrived," "completed," "spoke") that remains constant year-round mathematically drowned out the underlying seasonal operational signals.To solve this, we repurposed the deterministic text compression pipeline (EMI/PMI) by altering the categorical partition. Rather than partitioning the data by organizational boundaries, we partitioned a single department's historical data by time ($C = Season$).

```{r}
#| label: workflow-seasonal-scripts
#| eval: false
#| echo: false
# ==============================================================================
# Workflow Tracking: 
# The interactive table and LLM outputs below are generated via:
source("R/extract_seasonal_pmi.R")
source("R/generalized_seasonal_pipeline.R")
# ==============================================================================
```

#### 2.6.3.1 Isolating Seasonal Vocabulary for Public Works (`PWDx`)

By isolating the Public Works (PWDx) department and applying the seasonal partition, the EMI algorithm successfully vaporized the year-round administrative noise. We then calculated the Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) to isolate words mathematically drawn to specific seasons.

The distribution of these positive PMI scores (@fig-seasonal-pmi) has a strict mathematical constraint of Information Theory. The equation for PMI is:
$$PMI(w, c) = \log_2 \left( \frac{P(w, c)}{P(w)P(c)} \right)$$
If a word is 100% exclusive to a single season, the joint probability $P(w, c)$ equals the word probability $P(w)$, simplifying the equation to $\log_2(1 / P(c))$. 

As established in the previous capacity analysis (@fig-dept-stress), `PWDx` ticket volume is imbalanced, surging during the summer months. Because $P(c)$ varies by season, the raw mathematical ceiling for PMI fluctuates. To resolve this and allow for direct cross-seasonal comparison, we divide the raw scores by their respective theoretical maxima to calculate the Normalized PMI (NPMI). This normalization bounds the absolute maximum score at 1.0 across all four seasons.

Notice the far-right edge of the Winter facet in the resulting distribution (@fig-seasonal-pmi). The pronounced upward spike hitting this 1.0 maximum indicates a cluster of vocabulary that is exclusive to the winter months, providing an isolated operational signal.

```{r}
#| label: fig-seasonal-pmi
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of positive NPMI scores for PWDx by season. Notice the strict mathematical ceiling at 1.0, representing words that are 100% exclusive to a single season."

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidytext)
library(lubridate)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)

boston_data <- read_csv("../data/boston_clean.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

prep_data <- boston_data %>%
  filter(department == "PWDx", !is.na(closure_reason), !is.na(open_dt)) %>%
  mutate(
    month_num = month(open_dt),
    season = case_when(
      month_num %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "Winter",
      month_num %in% c(3, 4, 5)  ~ "Spring",
      month_num %in% c(6, 7, 8)  ~ "Summer",
      month_num %in% c(9, 10, 11) ~ "Fall"
    ),
    season = factor(season, levels = c("Winter", "Spring", "Summer", "Fall"))
  )

tokens <- prep_data %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, closure_reason) %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "^[a-z]+$")) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")

N_total <- nrow(tokens)
prob_season <- tokens %>% count(season, name = "N_c") %>% mutate(P_c = N_c / N_total)
prob_word <- tokens %>% count(word, name = "N_w") %>% filter(N_w >= 10) %>% mutate(P_w = N_w / N_total)

mi_data <- tokens %>%
  semi_join(prob_word, by = "word") %>%
  count(word, season, name = "N_wc") %>%
  mutate(P_wc = N_wc / N_total) %>%
  inner_join(prob_season, by = "season") %>%
  inner_join(prob_word, by = "word") %>%
  mutate(
    pmi = log2(P_wc / (P_w * P_c)),
    max_pmi = -log2(P_c),
    npmi = pmi / max_pmi,
    emi_component = (P_wc) * pmi 
  )

word_emi <- mi_data %>% group_by(word) %>% summarise(emi = sum(emi_component), .groups = "drop")

plot_data <- mi_data %>%
  inner_join(word_emi, by = "word") %>%
  filter(emi > 0, npmi > 0)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = npmi, fill = season)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, color = "black", linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ season, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 6)) +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "log1p", breaks = c(0, 1, 10, 100, 1000), labels = scales::comma) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title = "The Signal Filter: Normalized Mutual Information by Season",
    subtitle = "Inspecting the right tail for structural signal density.",
    x = "Normalized Pointwise Mutual Information",
    y = "Number of Words (log1p scale)"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "grey30"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```

The interactive table @tbl-pwdx-seasonal-all provides the extracted seasonal vocabulary for the Public Works department `PWDx`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pwdx-seasonal-all

#| warning: false

library(DT)

# Load the comprehensive seasonal PMI data
seasonal_all <- read_csv("../data/PWDx_seasonal_pmi_all.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Generate the interactive DataTable
datatable(
```

#### 2.6.3.2 Vocabulary Interpretation via LLM (Ollama)

To translate these mathematical vectors into operational insights, we conducted a blind test utilizing a local Large Language Model (LLM). The top 30 structural words ($n=30$) for each season were fed to the LLM without informing the model that the tokens belonged to a Public Works department. 

To evaluate the stability of the generative translation, the exact same prompt and parameters were executed twice (@tbl-llm-seasonal-profiles-1 and @tbl-llm-seasonal-profiles-2).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-llm-seasonal-profiles-1
#| tbl-cap: "Iteration 1: Generative Translation of Top 30 Seasonal PMI Tokens (PWDx)"
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

llm_call_1 <- read_csv("../data/PWDx_seasonal_llm_profiles_top30_call1.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

kable(llm_call_1, format = "html", escape = FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "15%") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "85%")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-llm-seasonal-profiles-2
#| tbl-cap: "Iteration 2: Generative Translation of Top 30 Seasonal PMI Tokens (PWDx)"
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

llm_call_2 <- read_csv("../data/PWDx_seasonal_llm_profiles_top30_call2.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

kable(llm_call_2, format = "html", escape = FALSE) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"), full_width = FALSE) %>%
  column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "15%") %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "85%")
```

By comparing the two iterations, we can directly observe both the deterministic power of the pipeline and the inherent vulnerabilities of Generative AI.

For three of the four seasons (Winter, Spring, Summer), the LLM outputs are nearly identical across both iterations. Because the high-PMI words extracted for these seasons were concrete physical nouns (e.g., plow, salt, icy, weed, resurface), the dense structural signals severely constrained the LLM's probability matrix. It was forced to produce highly accurate, stable translations of physical reality regardless of its probabilistic nature.

However, the Fall translation reveals a critical dynamic: semantic bleed when an AI is exposed to a mixed informational vector.

When inspecting the underlying mathematical array for Fall (see @tbl-pwdx-seasonal-all), the physical nouns (sweepers, machinery) are heavily diluted by a dense cluster of behavioral adjectives (genuinely, challenging, frustrating, prompt, feedback, eager).

Because LLMs function as narrative synthesis engines, they attempt to weave all provided tokens into a cohesive story. Across both iterations, rather than isolating the physical work, the model awkwardly merged the structural and behavioral tokens into a bizarre, anthropomorphized hybrid. It hallucinated a street sweeping and machinery crew focused on "recognizing the importance of minimizing frustration and staying eager" (Iteration 1), and addressing "difficulties and frustrations that may arise" (Iteration 2).

This behavior serves as a vital diagnostic tool. It proves that the PMI algorithm is highly sensitive; it did not just isolate the physical shift to Fall street sweeping, but simultaneously captured a localized administrative footprint (likely a management or customer service template heavily deployed to address complaints during those months). Ultimately, this demonstrates that while AI is a powerful semantic translator, deploying it without strict mathematical boundaries and human analytical oversight forces the model to synthesize noise, inevitably yielding operational hallucinations.

## 2.7 Operational Reliability (Survival Analysis)

While average resolution times are commonly used in municipal reporting, they suffer from a severe statistical flaw: survivorship bias. By excluding tickets that are currently open, standard averages artificially deflate the apparent resolution time of heavily backlogged departments.

To capture the true operational reliability of the city, we apply time-to-event Survival Analysis.

### 2.7.1 Kaplan-Meier Survival

Using the non-parametric Kaplan-Meier estimator, we plot the exact probability that a constituent's request will remain unresolved as days pass, treating open tickets as censored data points.

```{r}
#| label: fig-survival-analysis-departments
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Kaplan-Meier survival curves estimating the probability a ticket remains open over time. Department abbreviations: BTDT (Transportation), INFO (Mayor's Hotline), ISD (Inspectional Services), PARK (Parks & Recreation), PROP (Property Management), PWDx (Public Works)."

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(survival)
library(broom)
library(stringr)
library(scales)

# Isolate the top 5 departments
top_5_depts <- sla_delta_data %>%
  count(department, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  pull(department)
survival_df <- sla_delta_data %>%
  filter(department %in% top_5_depts) %>%
  mutate(
    max_date = max(open_dt, na.rm = TRUE),
    calc_end_dt = if_else(is.na(closed_dt), max_date, closed_dt),
    duration_days = as.numeric(difftime(calc_end_dt, open_dt, units = "days")),
    status_ind = if_else(is.na(closed_dt), 0, 1)
  ) %>%
  filter(duration_days >= 0)
# Fit the Kaplan-Meier Model
km_fit <- survfit(Surv(duration_days, status_ind) ~ department, data = survival_df)
tidy_km <- tidy(km_fit) %>% mutate(clean_dept = str_remove(strata, "department="))
# Visualize the Hazard Curves
ggplot(tidy_km, aes(x = time, y = estimate, color = clean_dept)) +
  geom_step(linewidth = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 60)) + 
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(), limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Time-to-Resolution: Ticket Survival Analysis",
    subtitle = "The mathematical probability that a 311 request remains unresolved as days pass.",
    x = "Days Since Request Opened",
    y = "Probability Ticket is Still Open",
    color = "Department"
  ) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14))
```

The Kaplan-Meier estimation reveals stark differences in how municipal departments process their queues, highlighting both highly reactive workforces and structural bottlenecks:

**Public Works (PWDx)**: The orange curve plummets almost instantly, indicating that roughly 80% to 85% of their tickets are resolved within the first 48 to 72 hours. This mathematically depicts a workforce optimized for rapid, high-volume triage (e.g., immediate pothole patching, trash pickup).

**Baseline Cluster (BTDT, INFO, ISD)**: Transportation, the Mayor's Hotline, and Inspectional Services track closely together. They successfully clear about 75% of their open tickets within the first week. After that initial drop, they demonstrate a steady, predictable burn-down rate for more complex cases, approaching a near-zero unresolved rate by the 60-day mark.

**Parks and Recreation (PARK)**: The purple curve is the critical anomaly. While PARK resolves about half of its tickets in the first few days, the curve abruptly flattens into a concrete floor. By day 20, nearly 30% of their tickets remain open, and approximately 20% are essentially abandoned past the 60-day mark. This mathematical "long-tail" confirms that PARK does not suffer from a simple speed issue, but rather a structural inability to clear complex tickets, heavily implying capital budget constraints or a reliance on seasonal workforce unlocks.

### 2.7.2 Multivariate Drivers of Resolution (Cox Proportional Hazards)

While the Kaplan-Meier curves show us the overall survival rate of tickets by department, municipal operations do not exist in a vacuum. A ticket's resolution time is simultaneously influenced by the department assigned, the method the constituent used to report it, and whether it includes rich context like photographs.

To untangle these overlapping variables, we apply a Cox Proportional Hazards Model:
$$h(t\vert{}X) = h_0(t) \exp(\beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \dots + \beta_p X_p)$$
Where:

- $t$ represents the time elapsed (in days) since the request was opened.
- $h(t\vert{}X)$ is the hazard rate. In this operational context, it is the probability of the ticket successfully closing at time $t$, given a specific set of operational variables $X$.
- $h_0(t)$ is the baseline hazard, representing the underlying resolution speed of the system when all variables are held at their default reference levels.
- $X_1, \dots, X_p$ are the predictor variables (our covariates, such as department and reporting source).
- $\beta_1, \dots, \beta_p$ are the coefficients estimated by the regression model.

This multivariate regression exponentiates these coefficients ($\exp(\beta)$) to calculate a Hazard Ratio (HR) for each variable. In this context, a "hazard" is a positive event (closing the ticket).

- HR > 1: The variable mathematically accelerates resolution (e.g., an HR of 1.5 means the ticket is closed 50% faster than the baseline).
- HR < 1: The variable acts as a bottleneck, delaying resolution.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cox-regression-model-adjusted
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Hazard Ratios (Log Scale) isolating the impact of reporting sources and departments. Automated API integrations (e.g., 'Maximo Integration' used by the Boston 311 system) have been removed to isolate human workforce efficiency."

library(dplyr)
library(survival)
library(broom)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)
library(stringr)

# Prepare Data and Filter Automated Artifacts
cox_df <- sla_delta_data %>%
  filter(department %in% c("BTDT", "ISD", "INFO", "PARK", "PWDx")) %>%
  mutate(
    calc_end_dt = if_else(is.na(closed_dt), max(open_dt, na.rm = TRUE), closed_dt),
    duration_days = as.numeric(difftime(calc_end_dt, open_dt, units = "days")),
    status_ind = if_else(is.na(closed_dt), 0, 1),
    source_clean = if_else(is.na(source), "Unknown", as.character(source))
  ) %>%
  # Remove the Maximo API artifact to measure actual human work
  filter(duration_days > 0, !str_detect(source_clean, "Maximo"))
# Fit the Adjusted Cox Model
cox_model <- coxph(Surv(duration_days, status_ind) ~ department + source_clean, data = cox_df)
# Tidy and Exponentiate
tidy_cox <- tidy(cox_model, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) %>%
  filter(term != "") %>%
  mutate(
    clean_term = str_remove_all(term, "department|source_clean"),
    is_significant = if_else(p.value < 0.05, "Significant (p < .05)", "Not Significant"),
    clean_term = fct_reorder(clean_term, estimate)
  )
# Build the Log-Scaled Forest Plot
ggplot(tidy_cox, aes(x = estimate, y = clean_term, color = is_significant)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high), height = 0.2, linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Apply base-10 log scale for mathematically accurate visual distances
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5)) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Significant (p < .05)" = "#1b9e77", "Not Significant" = "#7570b3")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Multivariate Drivers of Ticket Resolution",
    subtitle = "Variables to the right (HR > 1) accelerate resolution. Variables to the left (HR < 1) delay it.",
    x = "Hazard Ratio (Log-Scaled Multiplier of Resolution Speed)",
    y = "Operational Variable",
    color = "Statistical Significance"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.y = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11)
  )
```

In the multivariate forest plot, the central dashed line at $1.00$ establishes baseline resolution speed. Dots represent the Hazard Ratio (HR)—a direct speed multiplier. Variables to the right ($HR > 1$) accelerate resolution; those to the left ($HR < 1$) act as bottlenecks. The horizontal bars indicate 95% confidence intervals. Because none cross the baseline, we can state with 95% statistical confidence that these variables genuinely impact workforce velocity, rejecting the possibility of random anomalies.

**Public Works (PWDx)** operates at nearly double the baseline speed, validating its rapid triage design.

**Parks (PARK)** faces a 35% speed deficit from long-tail bottlenecks.

**INFO**: Manual intake channels like constituent phone calls introduce heavy administrative friction, slowing resolution pipelines by roughly 22% compared to digitally precise reporting via web portals.

## 2.8 System Stability: Queueing Theory and Backlog Velocity

While Survival Analysis evaluates the lifespan of individual tickets, it does not measure the aggregate dynamic health of a department. To diagnose systemic instability, we must shift from the ticket level to the macro system level using Queueing Theory. 

This approach relies strictly on the mathematical balance between the Arrival Rate ($\lambda$)—tickets opened—and the Service Rate ($\mu$)—tickets closed. By calculating the net weekly queue change, we can strip away subjective text and measure pure operational dynamics. When $\lambda > \mu$, the system enters a state of structural instability (growing backlog), regardless of how fast routine tickets are closed.

```{r}
#| label: fig-queue-velocity-analysis
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Queueing Stability: Weekly net change in unresolved tickets (Arrivals minus Services).Department abbreviations: BTDT (Transportation), INFO (Mayor's Hotline), ISD (Inspectional Services), PARK (Parks & Recreation), PROP (Property Management), PWDx (Public Works)."

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(lubridate)
library(tidyr)

# Calculate the Arrival Rate (lambda) and Service Rate (mu) per week
queue_dynamics <- sla_delta_data %>%
  filter(department %in% c("BTDT", "ISD", "INFO", "PARK", "PWDx")) %>%
  mutate(
    open_week = floor_date(open_dt, "week"),
    close_week = floor_date(closed_dt, "week")
  )
# Arrivals per week
arrivals <- queue_dynamics %>%
  group_by(department, week = open_week) %>%
  summarise(tickets_opened = n(), .groups = "drop")
# Services per week (ignoring NAs for open tickets)
services <- queue_dynamics %>%
  filter(!is.na(close_week)) %>%
  group_by(department, week = close_week) %>%
  summarise(tickets_closed = n(), .groups = "drop")
# Merge and calculate Net Backlog Velocity
backlog_velocity <- arrivals %>%
  full_join(services, by = c("department", "week")) %>%
  # Replace NAs with 0 for weeks where no tickets were opened or closed
  replace_na(list(tickets_opened = 0, tickets_closed = 0)) %>%
  mutate(
    net_queue_change = tickets_opened - tickets_closed,
    # Create a flag for color coding: Red = Growing queue, Blue = Shrinking queue
    status = if_else(net_queue_change > 0, "Queue Growing (Instability)", "Queue Recovering (Stability)")
  ) %>%
  # Filter out extreme edge dates if necessary to keep the plot clean
  filter(week >= min(arrivals$week, na.rm = TRUE) & week <= max(arrivals$week, na.rm = TRUE))
# Visualize the System Stability
ggplot(backlog_velocity, aes(x = week, y = net_queue_change, fill = status)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ department, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Queue Growing (Instability)" = "#e41a1c", 
                               "Queue Recovering (Stability)" = "#377eb8")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Departmental Queue Stability (Backlog Velocity)",
    subtitle = "Tracking weekly thermodynamic balance: Tickets Opened vs. Tickets Closed.",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Net Change in Open Tickets",
    fill = "System Status"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    legend.position = "top",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

The Backlog Velocity chart maps the behavioral pulse of the city's workforce without relying on subjective administrative text. It reveals distinct operational realities across the monitored departments:

**PARK**: For the first six months of the year, the Parks Department operates in an unbroken state of structural instability. The continuous red growth confirms they lack the baseline daily capacity to match inbound requests. The massive blue correction in July aligns perfectly with the July 1st start of the Boston municipal Fiscal Year. This strongly suggests a seasonal budget unlock, potentially allowing the department to finally deploy the capital or short-term seasonal workforce required to crush the six-month backlog.

**BTDT**: Transportation displays a massive, singular correction of over 1,500 closed tickets in late summer. Because human workforces do not organically resolve 1,500 complex street-level issues in a single week, this mathematical signature strongly suggests an artifact of database batch-closure. It might represent a forced administrative reset to clear a runaway queue rather than natural operational velocity.

**PWDx & INFO**: Public Works and the Mayor's Hotline constantly oscillate between small delays and immediate recoveries, closely hugging the baseline. This suggests highly reactive, well-managed workforces operating with zero structural slack. They seem to absorb immediate shocks (such as the January weather surge for PWDx) and immediately deploy surge capacity the following week to reset to zero.

**ISD**: Inspectional Services demonstrates a steady accumulation of backlog through the spring months, directly aligning with the seasonal surge in construction and housing permits. Sustained recovery does not begin until mid-summer, indicating a persistent, multi-month lag between peak citizen demand and peak service delivery.

## 2.9 Spatial Equity (Geospatial Autocorrelation)

While overall departmental velocity provides a measure of system health, it does not address the distribution of that service. A critical mandate of municipal operations is equitable service delivery across all neighborhoods.

To mathematically test if operational failures are equitably distributed or geographically biased, we apply spatial autocorrelation using Global Moran’s I [@moran1950notes; @li2007beyond]. By mapping the SLA breach rates (the percentage of tickets that miss their target resolution time) across Boston's spatial boundaries, we can identify statistically significant "cold spots"—clusters of neighborhoods that systematically receive delayed service compared to the citywide baseline.

### 2.9.1 Mapping SLA Breach Clusters

To mathematically test if operational failures are equitably distributed or geographically biased, we apply spatial autocorrelation using Global Moran’s I. The statistic compares the variance of SLA breach rates across neighboring areas against the overall citywide variance:
$$I = \frac{N}{W} \frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}$$
Where:

* $N$ is the total number of spatial units (in this case, census tracts) indexed by $i$ and $j$.
* $x_i$ and $x_j$ are the SLA breach rates for tracts $i$ and $j$, respectively.
* $\bar{x}$ is the citywide average SLA breach rate.
* $w_{ij}$ is the spatial weight matrix determining how tract $i$ and tract $j$ are connected (typically $1$ if they share a physical border, and $0$ if they do not).
* $W$ is the sum of all spatial weights ($W = \sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}$).

An index near $0$ implies that service delays are completely random ("equitable failure"). A positive index approaching $1$ proves that SLA breaches are structurally clustered, creating "cold spots" of systematic neglect. 

```{r}
#| label: fig-spatial-equity-morans-i
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Geospatial distribution of SLA breach rates across Boston census tracts."

library(dplyr)
library(sf)
library(tigris)
library(spdep)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)

# Gets the Shapefile via API (Natively downloads Suffolk County Census Tracts)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
boston_tracts <- tracts(state = "MA", county = "Suffolk", cb = TRUE, year = 2022, progress_bar = FALSE) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 4326)
# Prepare the 311 Spatial Points
spatial_311 <- sla_delta_data %>%
  filter(!is.na(latitude), !is.na(longitude)) %>%
  filter(!str_detect(if_else(is.na(source), "Unknown", as.character(source)), "Maximo")) %>%
  mutate(is_breach = if_else(on_time == "ONTIME", 0, 1)) %>% 
  # Convert flat data frame into an active spatial object
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)
# Spatial Join: Assign tickets to Census Tracts and calculate breach rates
tract_breaches <- boston_tracts %>%
  st_join(spatial_311, left = FALSE) %>%
  group_by(GEOID) %>%
  summarise(
    total_tickets = n(),
    breach_rate = mean(is_breach, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  # Filter out tracts with highly volatile low sample sizes (e.g., airport, harbor islands)
  filter(total_tickets > 50)
# Calculate Global Moran's I for Spatial Autocorrelation
# Create the spatial weights matrix (defining which tracts touch each other)
neighbors <- poly2nb(tract_breaches, queen = TRUE)
weights <- nb2listw(neighbors, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
# Execute the mathematical test
moran_result <- moran.test(tract_breaches$breach_rate, weights, zero.policy = TRUE)
# Visualization
ggplot(tract_breaches) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = breach_rate), color = "white", size = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Spatial Equity of Municipal Services",
    subtitle = paste0("Global Moran's I: ", round(moran_result$estimate[1], 3), 
                      " (p-value: ", signif(moran_result$p.value, 3), ")"),
    fill = "SLA Breach Rate"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = "right"
  )
```

@fig-spatial-equity-morans-i shows that the spatial distribution of service delays is far from random. The calculated Global Moran's I statistic of 0.25, coupled with a $p$-value of $1.37 \times 10^{-9}$, mathematically rejects the null hypothesis of spatial randomness. 

Visually, the map strongly corroborates this test: census tracts experiencing severe SLA breach rates (the bright orange and yellow zones exceeding 30%) are geographically contiguous, forming structural "hotspots" of operational delay. Conversely, neighborhoods receiving highly efficient service (the dark purple and black zones hovering around a 10% breach rate) form their own distinct, localized clusters. This definitive spatial autocorrelation proves that the promptness of municipal service is systematically tied to geographic location.

### 2.9.2 Localized Clusters of Neglect (LISA)

Having proven that municipal delays are not uniformly distributed, we apply Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) [@anselin1995local] to mathematically draw boundaries around the city's operational "hotspots" and "coldspots." By scaling the breach rates and calculating their spatial lags, we can isolate census tracts that suffer from statistically significant, systemic neglect.


```{r}
#| label: fig-spatial-equity-lisa
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "LISA Cluster Map isolating statistically significant zones of systemic neglect (High-High) and exceptional service (Low-Low)."
# Calculate Local Moran's I
local_m <- localmoran(tract_breaches$breach_rate, weights, zero.policy = TRUE)
# Scale the variables to determine the quadrants (centered on the mean)
c_breach <- tract_breaches$breach_rate - mean(tract_breaches$breach_rate, na.rm = TRUE)
c_lag <- lag.listw(weights, c_breach, zero.policy = TRUE)
# Categorize the tracts into LISA clusters
lisa_tracts <- tract_breaches %>%
  mutate(
    # Extract the p-value from the local moran matrix (Column 5)
    p_val = local_m[, 5], 
    # Define the raw spatial quadrants
    quadrant = case_when(
      c_breach > 0 & c_lag > 0 ~ "High-High (Systemic Neglect)",
      c_breach < 0 & c_lag < 0 ~ "Low-Low (Exceptional Service)",
      c_breach > 0 & c_lag < 0 ~ "High-Low (Spatial Outlier)",
      c_breach < 0 & c_lag > 0 ~ "Low-High (Spatial Outlier)",
      TRUE ~ "Not Significant"
    ),
    # Mask the quadrants by statistical significance (p < 0.05)
    lisa_cluster = if_else(p_val <= 0.05, quadrant, "Not Significant")
  ) %>%
  # Convert the cluster to a factor for ordered plotting
  mutate(lisa_cluster = factor(lisa_cluster, levels = c(
    "High-High (Systemic Neglect)", 
    "Low-Low (Exceptional Service)", 
    "High-Low (Spatial Outlier)", 
    "Low-High (Spatial Outlier)", 
    "Not Significant"
  )))
# Map the LISA Clusters
# Define a stark, color-blind friendly palette to highlight the inequity
lisa_colors <- c(
  "High-High (Systemic Neglect)" = "#d73027",    # Red
  "Low-Low (Exceptional Service)" = "#4575b4",   # Blue
  "High-Low (Spatial Outlier)" = "#fdae61",      # Light Orange
  "Low-High (Spatial Outlier)" = "#abd9e9",      # Light Blue
  "Not Significant" = "#f0f0f0"                  # Light Grey
)
ggplot(lisa_tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = lisa_cluster), color = "darkgrey", size = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = lisa_colors, drop = FALSE) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Zones of Systemic Neglect vs. Exceptional Service",
    subtitle = "Statistically significant spatial clusters of 311 SLA breaches (Local Moran's I, p < 0.05).",
    fill = "LISA Classification"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, hjust = 0.5),
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

@fig-spatial-equity-lisa reveals the precise neighborhood boundaries of systemic operational failures, moving beyond simple density to mathematically isolate zones of structural inequality.

The LISA analysis identifies three distinct "High-High" clusters of systemic neglect (highlighted in red) that are geographically separated from the city's central core:

**Western Cluster (Allston-Brighton)**: The largest contiguous zone of delayed service dominates the far western edge of the city.

**Northeast Cluster (East Boston)**: A secondary significant zone of systemic delay encompasses the northeast peninsula, bounded by Boston Harbor.

**Northern Cluster (Charlestown)**: A third, smaller pocket of concentrated SLA breaches is situated on the northern peninsula across the Charles River.

Conversely, the tracts classified as "Low-Low" (highlighted in blue)—indicating localized clusters of exceptionally prompt service delivery—are positioned centrally, situated within and immediately adjacent to the downtown municipal core. This spatial reality demonstrates that while service delays are not randomly distributed, they form distinct, localized geographic pockets that merit targeted operational review.

Data Cleaning

```{r}
#| label: data-cleaning-a
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| eval: false

# Ingestion
boston_311 <- read_csv(here("data", "tmpm461rr5o.csv"))

# Step 1: Base Filtering and Feature Engineering
boston_mutated <- boston_311 %>%
  # Filter for completed work orders
  filter(case_status == "Closed", !is.na(closed_dt), !is.na(open_dt)) %>%
  mutate(
    # Exact resolution time
    resolution_days = as.numeric(difftime(closed_dt, open_dt, units = "days")),
    # Temporal features for seasonality and scheduling analysis
    open_month = month(open_dt, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE),
    open_wday = wday(open_dt, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE, week_start = 1), # Monday = 1
    open_hour = hour(open_dt)
  )

# Step 2: Quantify the data entry errors
negative_records_count <- sum(boston_mutated$resolution_days < 0, na.rm = TRUE)

# Step 3: Purge errors and finalize the Resolved Cohort
boston_clean <- boston_mutated %>%
  filter(resolution_days >= 0)

write_csv(boston_clean, here("data", "boston_clean.csv"))

# Output the validation summary
cat("Purged", format(negative_records_count, big.mark = ","), "records with negative resolution times (data entry errors).\n")
cat("Cleaned dataset contains", format(nrow(boston_clean), big.mark = ","), "closed records ready for analysis.\n")
```

Hartigan's Dip Test

```{r}
#| label: hartigans-dip-test-a
#| eval: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hold

library(diptest)
library(dplyr)

# Test on the continuous days open variable
dip_result <- dip.test(boston_open$days_open_at_yearend)
# Extract and format the results
dip_stat <- round(dip_result$statistic, 4)
dip_pval <- format(dip_result$p.value, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)
# Consolidate output into a single string
conclusion_text <- if(dip_result$p.value < 0.05) {
  "Conclusion: The p-value approaches zero, mathematically rejecting unimodality.\nThe distinct waves in the backlog are structural realities, not binning artifacts."
} else {
  "Conclusion: Failed to reject unimodality."
}

final_output <- paste0(
  "--- Hartigan's Dip Test for Unimodality ---\n",
  "Dip Statistic (D): ", dip_stat, "\n",
  "P-Value:           ", dip_pval, "\n\n",
  conclusion_text, "\n"
)
cat(final_output)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ks-statistic-explanation-a

# 1. Identify a "Goldilocks" subgroup (high volume, moderate D_k around 0.35)
global_dist <- sla_delta_data$sla_delta_days

illustrative_group <- sla_delta_data %>%
  group_by(type) %>%
  filter(n() > 5000) %>% 
  summarise(
    ks_stat = suppressWarnings(ks.test(sla_delta_days, global_dist)$statistic),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(diff_from_target = abs(ks_stat - 0.35)) %>%
  arrange(diff_from_target) %>%
  slice(1)

max_type_name <- illustrative_group$type
max_type_dist <- sla_delta_data %>% filter(type == max_type_name) %>% pull(sla_delta_days)

# 2. Calculate the exact point of maximum vertical distance
x_vals <- sort(unique(c(global_dist, max_type_dist)))
ecdf_global_vals <- ecdf(global_dist)(x_vals)
ecdf_max_vals <- ecdf(max_type_dist)(x_vals)

diffs <- abs(ecdf_global_vals - ecdf_max_vals)
max_idx <- which.max(diffs)

x_max_diff <- x_vals[max_idx]
y_global <- ecdf_global_vals[max_idx]
y_max <- ecdf_max_vals[max_idx]
max_d_stat <- diffs[max_idx]

# Define dynamic labels to map math notation to the data
global_label <- "F_global : Global Baseline"
subgroup_label <- paste0("F_k : '", max_type_name, "' (Factor: type)")

# 3. Create the dataset for plotting
plot_data <- sla_delta_data %>%
  mutate(Curve = global_label) %>%
  bind_rows(
    sla_delta_data %>%
      filter(type == max_type_name) %>%
      mutate(Curve = subgroup_label)
  )

# 4. Generate the explanatory plot
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = sla_delta_days, color = Curve)) +
  stat_ecdf(linewidth = 1) +
  # Add the vertical segment illustrating D_k
  annotate("segment", x = x_max_diff, xend = x_max_diff,
           y = y_global, yend = y_max,
           color = "darkred", linewidth = 1.2, 
           arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.1, "inches"))) +
  # Annotate the exact D_k value mathematically
  annotate("text", x = x_max_diff + 2, y = mean(c(y_global, y_max)),
           label = paste0("D[k] == ", round(max_d_stat, 3)), parse = TRUE,
           color = "darkred", hjust = 0, size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  # Reference line for the SLA deadline (0 days)
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "black", linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.5) +
  # Map colors directly to the new dynamic labels
  scale_color_manual(values = setNames(c("darkgray", "steelblue"), c(global_label, subgroup_label))) +
  # Lock the zoom back to the critical operational window
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-30, 30)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Visualizing the Kolmogorov-Smirnov Statistic",
    subtitle = "The D_k statistic represents the maximum absolute vertical distance between the global distribution\nand a specific subgroup (in this example, the 'Parking Enforcement' level of the 'type' factor).",
    x = "SLA Delta (Days)",
    y = "Cumulative Proportion of Tickets Closed",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold")
  )
```

Volume-weighted Kolmogorov-Smirnov test

```{r}
#| label: feature-dependency-ks-a
#| eval: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

# Global baseline distribution
global_dist <- sla_delta_data$sla_delta_days
total_n <- nrow(sla_delta_data)
factors_to_test <- c("subject", "reason", "type", "queue", "department", 
                     "fire_district", "pwd_district", "city_council_district", 
                     "police_district", "neighborhood", "neighborhood_services_district", 
                     "ward", "precinct", "location_zipcode", "source")
# Function to calculate the Weighted K-S Distance and extract p-values
calc_weighted_ks <- function(factor_name, data, global_dist, total_n) {
  data %>%
    group_split(!!sym(factor_name)) %>%
    map_dfr(function(df) {
      level_dist <- df$sla_delta_days
      level_n <- nrow(df)
      # Skip virtually empty levels to prevent test errors
      if(level_n < 5) return(tibble(level_n = level_n, ks_stat = 0, p_val = 1))
      # Suppress warnings for expected ties
      ks_res <- suppressWarnings(ks.test(level_dist, global_dist))
      tibble(
        level_n = level_n,
        ks_stat = ks_res$statistic,
        p_val = ks_res$p.value
      )
    }) %>%
    summarise(
      Factor = factor_name,
      Weighted_KS_Score = sum(ks_stat * (level_n / total_n)),
      Median_P_Value = median(p_val)
    )
}
# Map across all factors and rank
ks_results <- map_dfr(factors_to_test, ~calc_weighted_ks(.x, sla_delta_data, global_dist, total_n)) %>%
  arrange(desc(Weighted_KS_Score)) %>%
  mutate(
    Weighted_KS_Score = round(Weighted_KS_Score, 4),
    Median_P_Value = format(Median_P_Value, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3)
  )
```

```{r}
  )
```

```{r}
  theme_minimal() +
```

#### Section 2.4.3 

@fig-variance-extremes

```{r}
#| label: fig-variance-extremes-a
#| eval: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Contrasting SLA Delta distributions of the fastest and slowest high-volume queues. The digital routing queue strictly dictates whether a task is systematically early or structurally delayed."

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(forcats)

# 1. Identify the best and worst performing high-volume queues
queue_summary <- sla_delta_data %>%
  group_by(queue) %>%
  summarise(
    total_tickets = n(),
    median_delta = median(sla_delta_days, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  # Isolate only robust, high-volume queues
  filter(total_tickets > 500)

# Extract the names of the top 5 and bottom 5 queues
fastest_queues <- queue_summary %>% slice_min(median_delta, n = 5) %>% pull(queue)
slowest_queues <- queue_summary %>% slice_max(median_delta, n = 5) %>% pull(queue)
target_queues <- c(fastest_queues, slowest_queues)

# 2. Filter the raw data and categorize for plotting
plot_data_extremes <- sla_delta_data %>%
  filter(queue %in% target_queues) %>%
  mutate(
    Performance = if_else(queue %in% fastest_queues, "Systematically Early", "Systematically Delayed"),
    # Reorder the factor based on median delay for a clean visual staircase
    queue = fct_reorder(queue, sla_delta_days, .fun = median, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Calculate dynamic axis limits to ensure all boxes fit (ignoring extreme 5% outliers)
x_lower <- quantile(plot_data_extremes$sla_delta_days, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
x_upper <- quantile(plot_data_extremes$sla_delta_days, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)

# 3. Generate the Boxplot
ggplot(plot_data_extremes, aes(x = sla_delta_days, y = queue, fill = Performance)) +
  # Suppress severe outliers, thicken whiskers (linewidth), and pop the median (fatten)
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8, outlier.alpha = 0.05, outlier.size = 0.5, 
               color = "black", linewidth = 0.6, fatten = 3) +
  # Reference line for the exact deadline
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 1.2) +
  # Use the dynamically calculated limits instead of hardcoded numbers
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(x_lower, x_upper)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Systematically Early" = "#4575b4", "Systematically Delayed" = "#d73027")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "The Operational Divide: Best vs. Worst Queues",
    subtitle = "Visualizing the K-S finding: The assigned digital queue dictates massive timeline variance.",
    x = "SLA Delta (Days)",
    y = NULL,
    fill = "Queue Performance"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold")
  )
```

##### Section 2.5.1.2

@tbl-llm-topic-translation

```{r}
#| label: tbla-llm-topic-translation
#| eval: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| cache: true
#| tbl-cap: "Automated Topic Translation via Local Llama 3 (Offline API)"

library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)
library(readr)
library(here)
library(knitr)
library(httr)

# CLEAN FIRST, then get the Top 15 Unique topics
ai_results <- read_csv(here("data", "boston_bertopic_results.csv"))
topic_summary <- ai_results %>%
  filter(topic_id != -1) %>%
  mutate(
    clean_raw_topic = str_remove(ai_topic_name, "^\\d+_"),
    clean_raw_topic = str_replace_all(clean_raw_topic, "_", " ")
  ) %>%
  count(clean_raw_topic, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)
# Direct Local API with the Proper Persona
translate_topic <- function(messy_string) {
  sys_prompt <- "You are an expert municipal data analyst for the City of Boston. You classify messy 311 work order keywords."
  user_prompt <- paste0(
    "Translate this messy keyword string into a clean, 3-to-4 word operational category label (e.g., 'Equipment Maintenance', 'Duplicate Request').\n\n",
    "Return ONLY the label. Do not include quotes, formatting, or introductory text.\n\n",
    "Keyword: ", messy_string
  )
  # Send offline request directly to local Mac memory
  res <- tryCatch({
    POST(
      url = "http://localhost:11434/api/generate",
      body = list(
        model = "llama3",
        prompt = user_prompt,
        system = sys_prompt,
        stream = FALSE
      ),
      encode = "json",
      timeout(30)
    )
  }, error = function(e) return(NULL))
  if (is.null(res) || status_code(res) != 200) return("API Connection Failed")
  raw_text <- content(res, as = "parsed", type = "application/json")$response
  # Strip out any markdown or quotes the LLM tries to sneak in
  clean_label <- str_remove_all(raw_text, '["*]') %>% str_trim()
  return(as.character(clean_label))
}
# Loop through the 15 topics
llm_clean_names <- map_chr(topic_summary$clean_raw_topic, translate_topic)
# Build and print the crosswalk table
topic_crosswalk <- tibble(
  `Original c-TF-IDF String` = topic_summary$clean_raw_topic,
  `LLM Dashboard Label` = llm_clean_names
)
kable(topic_crosswalk, caption = "Automated Topic Translation via Local Llama 3 (Offline API)")
```

##### Section 2.5.1.3

@fig-topic-factor-enrichment

```{r}
#| label: fig-topic-factor-enrichment-a
#| eval: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Enrichment heatmap showing which AI topics are statistically over-represented across municipal departments. Department abbreviations: BTDT (Transportation), INFO (Mayor's Hotline), ISD (Inspectional Services), PARK (Parks & Recreation), PROP (Property Management), PWDx (Public Works)."

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(here)

# Load the AI results and join the LLM translated labels
ai_df <- read_csv(here("data", "boston_bertopic_results.csv")) %>%
  filter(topic_id != -1, !is.na(department)) %>%
  mutate(
    clean_raw_topic = str_remove(ai_topic_name, "^\\d+_"),
    clean_raw_topic = str_replace_all(clean_raw_topic, "_", " ")
  ) %>%
  # Bring in the translations from the previous chunk
  left_join(topic_crosswalk, by = c("clean_raw_topic" = "Original c-TF-IDF String")) %>%
  mutate(
    # Fallback to the title-cased raw topic if it wasn't in our Top 15 translated list
    Final_Label = ifelse(is.na(`LLM Dashboard Label`), str_to_title(clean_raw_topic), `LLM Dashboard Label`)
  )
# Focus on top departments and top topics to keep the grid readable
top_depts  <- ai_df %>% count(department, sort = TRUE) %>% slice_head(n = 6) %>% pull(department)
top_topics <- ai_df %>% count(Final_Label, sort = TRUE) %>% slice_head(n = 12) %>% pull(Final_Label)
filtered_df <- ai_df %>%
  filter(department %in% top_depts, Final_Label %in% top_topics)
# Create a contingency table and run Chi-Square to get Standardized Residuals
contingency_matrix <- table(filtered_df$Final_Label, filtered_df$department)
chisq_res <- chisq.test(contingency_matrix)
# Convert residuals back to a tidy dataframe for ggplot
enrichment_data <- as.data.frame(chisq_res$stdres) %>%
  rename(Topic = Var1, Department = Var2, StdResidual = Freq)
# Visualize as an Enrichment Heatmap using the clean LLM labels
ggplot(enrichment_data, aes(x = Department, y = Topic, fill = StdResidual)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2b83ba", mid = "#ffffbf", high = "#d7191c",
    midpoint = 0,
    name = "Standardized\nResidual"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Enrichment of AI Topics Across Departments",
    subtitle = "Red indicates strong over-representation (residual > +2); Blue indicates under-representation.",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, face = "bold"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold")
  )
```

@fig-emi-distribution

```{r}
#| label: fig-emi-distribution-a
#| eval: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 10
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of Expected Mutual Information (EMI) word counts, with factors ordered from top-left to bottom-right by decreasing mean EMI."

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(scales)
library(readr)

mi_results <- read_csv("../data/mi_results.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# 1. Calculate mean Expected MI per factor to establish a decreasing sort order
factor_ranking <- mi_results %>%
  group_by(factor) %>%
  summarise(mean_emi = mean(expected_mi, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_emi)) %>%
  pull(factor)

# 2. Create the "Global" summary pseudo-factor (Max EMI across all factors for each word)
global_mi <- mi_results %>%
  group_by(word) %>%
  summarise(expected_mi = max(expected_mi, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(factor = "Global (Max EMI)")

# 3. Combine data and set factor levels: Global first, followed by factors ordered by mean EMI
plot_data <- bind_rows(global_mi, mi_results) %>%
  mutate(factor = factor(factor, levels = c("Global (Max EMI)", factor_ranking)))

# 4. Generate the 4x2 faceted plot
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = expected_mi, fill = factor)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, color = "black", linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ factor, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  # Log-transform the X-axis to spread out the dense region near zero
  scale_x_continuous(
    trans = "log1p",
    breaks = c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2),
    labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.01)
  ) +
  # Log-transform the Y-axis counts
  scale_y_log10(
    labels = scales::comma,
    breaks = c(1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000)
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title = "The Signal Filter: Expected Mutual Information Distribution",
    subtitle = "Factors ordered by decreasing mean Expected MI, highlighting structural information density.",
    x = "Expected Mutual Information (log1p bits)",
    y = "Number of Words (log scale)",
    fill = "Factor"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "grey30"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )
```

```{r}
    cols = c(Total_Demand, SLA_Breaches),
    names_to = "Metric",
    values_to = "Volume"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Metric = factor(Metric, levels = c("Total_Demand", "SLA_Breaches"), 
                    labels = c("Total Inbound Tickets (Demand)", "Missed SLAs (System Failure)"))
  )
# Build the faceted visualization
ggplot(dept_summary, aes(x = created_month, y = Volume, group = Metric, color = Metric)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ department, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Total Inbound Tickets (Demand)" = "#b3cde3", 
                                "Missed SLAs (System Failure)" = "#e41a1c")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Stress Test by Top Departments",
    subtitle = "Comparing capacity thresholds across individual workflows (Note: Y-axes vary by department).",
    x = "Month Request Opened",
    y = "Ticket Volume",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    legend.position = "top",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

##### Section 2.6.3.1 

@fig-seasonal-pmi

```{r}
#| label: fig-seasonal-pmi-a
#| eval: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of positive PMI scores for PWDx by season. Notice the strict mathematical ceiling near 2.0, representing words that are 100% exclusive to a single season."

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidytext)
library(lubridate)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)

boston_data <- read_csv("../data/boston_clean.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

prep_data <- boston_data %>%
  filter(department == "PWDx", !is.na(closure_reason), !is.na(open_dt)) %>%
  mutate(
    month_num = month(open_dt),
    season = case_when(
      month_num %in% c(12, 1, 2) ~ "Winter",
      month_num %in% c(3, 4, 5)  ~ "Spring",
      month_num %in% c(6, 7, 8)  ~ "Summer",
      month_num %in% c(9, 10, 11) ~ "Fall"
    ),
    season = factor(season, levels = c("Winter", "Spring", "Summer", "Fall"))
  )

tokens <- prep_data %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, closure_reason) %>%
  filter(str_detect(word, "^[a-z]+$")) %>%
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word")

N_total <- nrow(tokens)
prob_season <- tokens %>% count(season, name = "N_c") %>% mutate(P_c = N_c / N_total)
prob_word <- tokens %>% count(word, name = "N_w") %>% filter(N_w >= 10) %>% mutate(P_w = N_w / N_total)

mi_data <- tokens %>%
  semi_join(prob_word, by = "word") %>%
  count(word, season, name = "N_wc") %>%
  mutate(P_wc = N_wc / N_total) %>%
  inner_join(prob_season, by = "season") %>%
  inner_join(prob_word, by = "word") %>%
  mutate(
    pmi = log2(P_wc / (P_w * P_c)),
    emi_component = (P_wc) * pmi 
  )

word_emi <- mi_data %>% group_by(word) %>% summarise(emi = sum(emi_component), .groups = "drop")

plot_data <- mi_data %>%
  inner_join(word_emi, by = "word") %>%
  filter(emi > 0, pmi > 0)

ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = pmi, fill = season)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, color = "black", linewidth = 0.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ season, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 6)) +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = "log1p", breaks = c(0, 1, 10, 100, 1000), labels = scales::comma) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title = "The Signal Filter: Pointwise Mutual Information by Season",
    subtitle = "Inspecting the right tail for structural signal density.",
    x = "Pointwise Mutual Information (Bits)",
    y = "Number of Words (log1p scale)"
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "grey30"),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    legend.position = "none"
  )
```
